title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6400983 — U K Insurance Limited
text:
DRN-6400983

The complaint

Ms G is unhappy that U K Insurance Limited (“UKI”) unfairly handled a claim on her buildings
insurance policy following a leak from the flat upstairs.

What happened
Ms G and her late mother were joint policyholders of a buildings insurance policy with UKI. In
June 2024, they made a claim following a leak from the flat upstairs which damaged their
property.

UKI accepted the claim but couldn’t progress the repairs because the owner of the flat
upstairs was disputing liability, the cause of the leak couldn’t be established, and it wasn’t
fixed for a long time. This was finally resolved in February 2025. Ms G’s mother sadly died
around the same time and Ms G continued with the claim.

UKI arranged drying and repair works. During the repairs, a shower room ceiling was
replaced. Ms G became concerned that the ceiling hadn’t been replaced using moisture-
resistant plasterboard and that fungicidal treatment hadn’t been applied to the ceiling timbers
in line with the scope of works. She was also unhappy with how long UKI’s recovery process
was taking against the owner upstairs and wanted her excess back.

UKI accepted that moisture-resistant plasterboard should’ve been used. It offered Ms G
£390 to reflect the cost of putting that right. Ms G didn’t think £390 was enough. She has
relevant professional expertise and estimated the work would cost £950. UKI didn’t agree
and invited Ms G to accept £390 or provide an independent quote.

UKI also said fungicidal treatment to the timbers wasn’t required. And in relation to its
recovery process, it acknowledged that this had taken a long time but said it couldn’t pursue
a recovery of its costs until the source of the leak had been found and repaired. UKI also
acknowledged some service failings during the handling of the claim and paid £400 to
apologise.

Unhappy with UKI’s response, Ms G referred the matter to our Service. Our Investigator
didn’t think the complaint should be upheld. Ms G didn’t agree and later provided an
independent estimate from a consulting firm who calculated the work would cost £2,461.50.

As the matter remained unresolved, it came to me to decide. I issued a provisional decision
explaining why I intended to uphold the complaint and direct UKI to pay Ms G £950, plus
interest, in relation to the ceiling. I said:

“The cash settlement offer

UKI accepts that moisture-resistant plasterboard should’ve been used when it replaced the
shower room ceiling. The issue I need to decide is whether £390 fairly reflects the cost of
putting that right.

Having considered the available evidence, including the recent estimate Ms G has provided,
I’m not persuaded that £390 is fair. I’ll explain why.

I’ve looked carefully at how UKI arrived at that figure. It’s provided a breakdown to show that
it included:

•
Protecting work surfaces
•
Standard plasterboard and skimming the ceiling
•
Repainting affected walls
•
Painting the new ceiling
However, that work doesn’t appear to include the removal of the existing ceiling or disposal
of any waste. Nor does it include cleaning, or electrical work to the ceiling lights that was
included in the original scope of works. And crucially it doesn’t include the extra cost of
moisture-resistant plasterboard, which was the reason the offer was made.

It’s also based on the cost for UKI’s large network contractor. Our Service generally takes
the view that this is a fair approach when an insurer has offered to arrange the work and the
policyholder has chosen a cash settlement instead. But I haven’t seen evidence that UKI has
offered to arrange the work. Instead, it chose a cash payment to resolve the issue. So, in my
view the offer should’ve been based on the cost Ms G was likely to incur in the open market.

With that in mind, I don’t think £390 is a fair or reliable figure.

I’ve thought carefully about the fair way to resolve this issue.

Ms G has consistently said the work would cost £950. She’s said this is based on the cost of
labour in her area, materials, and other associated costs. While she hasn’t provided a
detailed breakdown, I don’t think it would be fair to dismiss her estimate outright. She’s
professionally qualified to calculate the cost of work like this.

I’ve considered the recent estimate she’s provided from a building consultant, of almost
£2,500. UKI rejected that estimate because it thought it included timber treatment. That’s not
right. The estimate doesn’t include timber treatment and confirms this on the first page. The
breakdown on the second page also doesn’t include timber treatment.

However, I don’t think that estimate fairly establishes the amount UKI should pay. First, it’s
almost three times more than Ms G’s own estimate. Second, it’s almost half the cost that UKI
paid for the entire project, which involved considerably more work (albeit with its network
contractor). And third, in situations like this, we’d usually expect the consumer to have
obtained a quote from a tradesman or company willing to do the work. I haven’t seen that the
consulting firm’s estimate was produced in that context.

So, I’m not convinced it would be fair for UKI to pay the cost of that estimate. Even so, the
estimate does strongly support my view that £390 is too low.

I’m conscious that this matter has gone on for a long time and that has been difficult for
Ms G. In the circumstances, I don’t think it would be fair to prolong the matter further by
requiring either party to get more quotations. Based on the available evidence, I think a
pragmatic outcome is needed to resolve the complaint fairly and allow the parties to move
forward. Given Ms G’s professional qualifications, the amount she’s consistently estimated
the works will cost, and the independent quote she’s provided, I’m satisfied on balance that
£950 represents a fair and reasonable amount to resolve the matter.

So, I’m intending to tell UKI to pay Ms G £950. UKI should add 8% simple yearly interest to
that amount from the date of its £390 offer until the date of settlement, to reflect the fact that
Ms G has been without money she otherwise should’ve had for that period.

In reaching this view, I’ve taken into account that UKI did invite Ms G to provide an
independent quote and didn’t simply offer the £390. However, that essentially left Ms G to
choose either an inadequate and incomplete cash settlement, or the burden of obtaining a
quote herself, which I don’t think was fair.

The timber treatment

Ms G says UKI should’ve carried out fungicidal treatment to the ceiling timbers after the leak.
I’ve considered this carefully, but I’m not persuaded that UKI has acted unfairly here.

UKI’s contractors inspected the timbers after the drying was completed. They concluded the
timbers were dry and didn’t need treatment. UKI has explained that the treatment was
included in the original scope of works on an ‘if required’ basis and was removed when the
contractors found it wasn’t needed.

Ms G believes the treatment should’ve been carried out anyway, even if as a precaution. I
understand that view. But I’m not persuaded the treatment was necessary here.

I’ve ultimately had to decide whose opinion I find more persuasive. In the circumstances, I’m
more persuaded by the opinion of the contractors who inspected the timbers after the drying
was completed. I also haven’t seen evidence that the timbers have gotten worse or that any
damage has been caused because they weren’t treated.

Even so, I do understand Ms G’s concerns about durability. UKI has said the works are
guaranteed, and we would expect repairs to be effective and lasting. So, if further damage is
found in future, Ms G will be able to raise that to UKI to investigate.

The recovery process

Ms G says UKI took too long to pursue its costs from the owner of the flat upstairs and their
insurer.

I’ve considered UKI’s internal records and I don’t think UKI acted unfairly.

The records show the owner of the flat upstairs didn’t agree that the leak came from their
flat. They suggested it came from the roof, yet Ms G was adamant it came from the flat
upstairs. As liability was in dispute and the leak was continuing, I don’t think UKI could
reasonably have taken action at that time. UKI told Ms G that it couldn’t force the owner to
repair the leak and could only try to recover costs after they’d been incurred, which I don’t
think was unreasonable.

The records show UKI kept recovery under review and discussed the matter with Ms G
several times. Once she told UKI in February 2025 that the leak had been established in the
upstairs flat and repaired, UKI pursued the matter against the upstairs owner. And once the
owner provided their insurer’s details, UKI wrote to them soon after.

I appreciate from Ms G’s point of view that the process should’ve started sooner, and she’d
like her excess back. UKI acknowledged the matter took longer than it would like, but I agree
with UKI’s position that it couldn’t reasonably pursue recovery any earlier. And, even if UKI

had started the recovery process earlier with the information it had, I haven’t seen any
evidence that Ms G would’ve recovered her excess any earlier.

So, I don’t intend to uphold this point.

Compensation

UKI has compensated Ms G £400 for its poor handling of the claim. This included not
responding to several emails and the issue with the plasterboard.

I’ve considered whether that’s a fair amount in the circumstances, and I think it is.

UKI has accepted there were failings in its handling of some parts of the claim. I agree that
those failings caused Ms G unnecessary frustration and inconvenience. I also recognise that
this has come about during a very difficult period for Ms G personally, following the loss of
her mother. The poor handling has no doubt added to the distress and uncertainty she was
already feeling.

However, taking everything into account, I’m satisfied that £400 is broadly in line with what I
would’ve awarded for what’s happened. So, I’m not intending to award more compensation.”

Responses

UKI said it accepted my provisional decision.

Ms G broadly accepted my provisional decision but noted it was silent on the return of her
policy excess. She asked that I address whether UKI should return that to her if it recovers
its costs from the third-party insurer. She asked how UKI should calculate that, how long the
process might take, and whether UKI should provide updates to her going forward.

As both parties have responded, I now consider it appropriate to issue my final decision.

What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and reasonable
in the circumstances of this complaint.
As both parties have accepted the substance of my provisional decision, I’ve found no
reason to reach a different conclusion.
I’ve considered Ms G’s comments about her policy excess. I understand why that’s important
to her. However, it isn’t a matter I can determine in this decision.
The complaint referred to our Service was that UKI had taken too long to deal with its
recovery process and as a result Ms G hadn’t received her excess back. In my provisional
decision, I explained why I was satisfied UKI had handled the recovery process fairly. My
findings covered UKI’s actions up to its final response letter of 4 July 2025.
While I understand Ms G wants certainty about what’ll happen next, it wouldn’t be
appropriate for me to direct UKI to take any particular actions in the future depending on
whether it makes a successful recovery.
UKI has said it will look to return Ms G’s excess if it recovers its costs. I can’t determine how
any future return of the excess should be calculated, how long it might or should take, or
what updates UKI should provide while that’s ongoing.

If Ms becomes unhappy with how UKI has handled, or goes on to handle, the matter after its
final response of 4 July 2025, she would be entitled to raise a new complaint to UKI and, if
necessary, could refer that complaint to our Service to independently investigate.
In all, I’ve reviewed the matter again and my opinion remains the same. So, my provisional
decision and my additional comments here now form this, my final decision.
Putting things right
To resolve the complaint, I direct UKI to:

•
pay Ms G £950 to resolve the moisture-resistant plasterboard issue, and

•
add 8% simple yearly interest to that amount, from the date UKI first offered Ms G
£390, until the date of settlement*.
*If UKI considers that it’s required by HM Revenue & Customs to deduct income tax from that interest, it should tell Ms G how
much it’s taken off. It should also give Ms G a tax deduction certificate if she asks for one, so she can reclaim the tax from HM
Revenue & Customs if appropriate.

My final decision
For the reasons I’ve given, I uphold Ms G’s complaint and direct U K Insurance Limited to do
as I’ve set out above.

Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Ms G to accept or
reject my decision before 1 July 2026.

Chris Woolaway
Ombudsman

title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6174836 — Fairmead Insurance Limited
text:
DRN-6174836

The complaint

Mr B complains about Fairmead Insurance Limited (“Fairmead”) for repairs done by its
contractors following a claim. He wants Fairmead to replace his property on a like for like
basis to put things right.
What happened
Any references to Mr B or Fairmead include respective agents or representatives.
Mr B insured his home with Fairmead.
Around 2016, Mr B installed new doors and a gate to his property as part of flood defences.
The company described themselves as carrying out flood guard work.
He had a double gate with compression seal and a removable threshold installed to the front
of his property. This abutted stone walls on either side.
In Spring 2023, a driver crashed into Mr B’s wall and gate and caused damage. He
submitted a claim to Fairmead.
Fairmead sent its assessor to the property to review the damage and to prepare a report.
The resulting report described that a vehicle had “snapped the flood gates to the front of the
driveway” and that the “gates and gate posts have been snapped off and will need to be
replaced with new. As they are flood gates this will require a specialist flood company to
replace the gates on a like for like basis.”
The report also detailed that the remainder of the stone wall would need to be removed and
a new wall built.
Fairmead accepted the claim and instructed contractors to carry out repairs.
The contractors completed work in November 2023, and Mr B complained shortly thereafter.
He observed that the replacement gates no longer functioned as flood gates as they had
around a 2-inch gap between the gate and gate posts, so any flood water would quickly
penetrate this.
He complained to Fairmead and requested that the gates be made functional as flood gates.
Fairmead responded in June 2024 rejecting Mr B’s complaint. It stated that it had not seen
evidence that his previous gates had been specialist flood gates such as to render the
replacement gates not a reasonable replacement.
Mr B was not happy and contacted us.
One of our investigators looked into this matter and recommended that the complaint be
upheld. They noted that the surveyor, who had assessed the gates and previous wall
damage, had been clear that in order to give an effective and lasting repair the replacement

gates needed to be resistant to flooding. This required that there be no spaces left open
when the gates were in the closed position. The investigator recommended that Fairmead
instruct a specialist to assess how to provide a flood gate, including if appropriate, adapting
the existing gate. The investigator also recommended that Fairmead pay to Mr B £200
compensation for his distress and inconvenience.
Fairmead did not accept that view and asked for an ombudsman decision. Mr B also
indicated that he did not want an adaptation of the current gate as parts of it had split and
the bolts were misaligned.
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and reasonable
in the circumstances of this complaint.
I have, in particular, considered my colleague’s view, Fairmead’s response to that view, and
the evidence provided by Mr B of the gate that was in place before the impact.
In this case there is no dispute that an insured event has taken place - and that Fairmead
has accepted the claim. The dispute surrounds the quality of the repair that Fairmead’s
agent have completed. Fairmead will be aware of the expectation this Service would have
that any repair be effective and lasting.
I agree entirely with my colleague’s view, that Fairmead has not, in this case, provided an
effective and lasting repair of the damaged gate and wall.
Mr B has provided evidence that the replacement gates were based on the dimensions of
the previous gate, but because the repairs to the wall and the gate posts (which were also
carried out by Fairmead’s contractors) changed the dimensions of the wall, the fit of the
replacement gates was in no way a flood gate, due to substantial gaps between the gate and
the gate posts on both sides which would allow water to penetrate.
Fairmead has argued that there is not sufficient evidence that Mr B had previously engaged
specialists, or that his previous gate was a flood gate. It argues that the previous gate was a
standard construction, and so a standard construction gate is a reasonable replacement.
I disagree with this argument. Mr B has provided the invoice for the original gates, from a
company which indicated, by its name, that it was a flood specialist, for a gate described as
a double gate with compression seal and removable threshold. I consider this sufficient
evidence that the previous gate was intended to be, and I accept Mr B’s account that it was,
an effective defence against flood water once in situ.
But even if I agreed with Fairmead – which I don’t - whether the gate was specifically a
specialist flood defence system or whether it was standard construction is not relevant, and it
makes no difference to the outcome I’ve reached in this case. I say this as, when installed in
the previous arrangement of walls and gate posts, the previous gate served as an effective
flood gate.
That is what Mr B lost. Fairmead’s assessor acknowledged that what had been in place
before the loss was a flood gate, and what was needed to indemnify Mr B was a flood gate.
The Scope of works prepared by the assessor clearly articulated that the work should
include “specialist to supply and fit new bespoke hand made flood gates and gate posts to
match existing”.
The replacement gate is not an effective flood gate due to the significant gapping around the

gate. Fairmead has therefore not properly indemnified Mr B for his loss, in line with the policy
cover.
Putting things right
I agree with my colleague’s assessment that in order to put matters right, Fairmead should
arrange for an independent flood gate specialist to assess the gates installed and design
and install gates for the front of his property without spaces - this could include using the
current gates to any extent the specialist may think appropriate.
I note that Mr B does not wish to have the existing gates adapted as he considers that the
quality of them is failing, but it is open to Fairmead to attempt a repair. Any repair or
replacement would be expected to last for a reasonable period and be effective and Mr B
would be entitled to complain if any resulting gate were still deficient.
Alternatively, Fairmead may allow Mr B to source his own assessment of the gates and
obtain a quote for installation / adaptation to make the gates into a functioning flood gate and
then pay that quote.
In addition, Fairmead should pay £200 compensation to Mr B for his distress and
inconvenience. He has described that he has suffered increased anxiety due to not having
appropriate defences around is home, during a period which was already difficult for him. I
agree that £200 is appropriate compensation for his additional distress and inconvenience
caused by the inadequate repair.
My final decision
For the reasons given above I uphold Mr B’s complaint and direct Fairmead Insurance
Limited to:
• Arrange for an independent flood gate specialist to assess the installed gates, and
design and install appropriate flood gates. This could include the current gates if the
specialist considers appropriate;
• Alternatively, allow Mr B to source his own flood gate specialist and obtain a quote
for installation of effective flood gates, and then pay that quote; and
• Pay to Mr B £200 compensation for his distress and inconvenience.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr B to accept or
reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

Laura Garvin-Smith
Ombudsman

title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6308662 — Frasers Group Financial Services Limited
text:
DRN-6308662

The complaint

Mr S complains that Frasers Group Financial Services Limited, trading as Studio (“Studio”)
lent to him irresponsibly.
What happened
In August 2017, Mr S successfully applied for a mail order credit account with Studio. He
was given an initial credit limit of £70.
Studio increased the credit limit on Mr S’ account on seven occasions over the next seven
years. The limit was first increased to £200 in May 2018. This remained until July 2023 when
it was increased to £400. It was increased twice more that year; to £550 in October and
£700 in December. In 2024 this was further increased to £850 in January, £975 in April, and
finally £1,000 in July.
In December 2025 Mr S complained to Studio.
Mr S says that Studio should not have lent to him as he was already in financial difficulty. He
says he has medical conditions that make managing finances extremely difficult. He argues
that Studio didn’t carry out appropriate affordability checks and lent to him irresponsibly.
Mr S is unhappy that Studio increased his credit limit over time and thinks this made his
financial situation worse. He says he was able to borrow more than he could reasonably
afford, which led to increased stress and further reliance on credit.
Mr S wants Studio to refund all interest and charges to his account.
Studio issued its final response on 29 January 2026.
They rejected Mr S’ complaint. They said that the checks carried out were proportionate and
that the lending decisions, including the credit limit increases, were fair.
Mr S disagreed with this outcome, and the complaint was referred to our service.
An investigator reviewed the complaint. They concluded that the checks carried out when
the account was opened were proportionate. They felt that additional information should
have been obtained before increasing the limit in May 2018, but concluded that even if
further checks had been carried out, this decision to lend would still have been fair. They
also thought the credit limit increases made between July 2023 and July 2024 were
reasonable. So, our investigator didn’t recommend that the complaint should be upheld.
Mr S didn’t agree with the investigator’s findings.
Because an agreement couldn’t be reached, the complaint has been passed to me to
decide.

What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Having done so, I’ve reached the same outcome as the investigator, largely for the same
reasons. I know this will disappoint Mr S, so I’ll explain why.
I’ve kept in mind the regulator’s rules and guidance on responsible lending (set out in its
Consumer Credit Sourcebook – CONC) which lenders, such as Studio, need to abide by.
Studio will be aware of these, and our approach to unaffordable/irresponsible lending
complaints is set out on our website. I’ve used this approach to decide Mr S’ complaint. I
won’t refer to the regulations in detail but will briefly summarise them.
The rules and regulations in place at the time Studio provided Mr S with the account required
them to carry out a reasonable and proportionate assessment to make sure he could afford
to repay what he owed in a sustainable way. This is sometimes referred to as an
‘affordability assessment’ or ‘affordability check’. Being able to sustainably repay credit
means that they needed to consider whether he could make repayments without undue
difficulty, while being able to meet any other commitments and without having to borrow
further.
There isn’t a ‘set list’ of checks that lenders must complete, but they must be proportionate
to the specific circumstances of the lending. What counts as a proportionate affordability
check will depend on the customer’s circumstances, such as their financial situation, history
and any signs of vulnerability. It may also depend on the type, amount and cost of credit, so
the customer is treated fairly.
The checks needed to be borrower focused. So Studio had to think not just about the
likelihood of them getting the funds back, or whether Mr S met their lending criteria. They
also had to consider if he could sustainably repay the lending being provided to him. I’ve
kept all of this in mind when thinking about whether Studio did what was needed, before
lending to Mr S.
Account opening
Studio completed a credit check for Mr S as part of the application, using a Credit Reference
Agency (CRA). They use this information to help them to decide whether to approve the
application or not. This is because the check shows how existing credit commitments with
other lenders are being managed. Studio say their checks were adequate and in line with
regulations.
The credit check showed Mr S was managing his existing credit well. There was no evidence
of County Court judgments (CCJs), individual voluntary arrangements (IVAs) or bankruptcy.
There was evidence of a payment arrangement, but there was no new negative information
in the last six months. I think it was reasonable for Studio to have treated this as historic, as
it did not appear to reflect Mr S’ financial circumstances at the time of the application.
I’m satisfied the checks carried out by Studio were proportionate and that it was reasonable
for them to approve the account. I say this because Mr S’ credit management appeared
positive at the time and the initial credit limit was modest.
Credit limit increases

I’ve also considered Mr S’ concerns about the changes Studio made to his credit limit. It is
clear that Studio initially offered Mr S a low credit limit and monitored the account before
they increased his borrowing.
As well as external information obtained from the CRA, Studio could now also look at how
well Mr S was managing his account with them, to assess whether or not he could afford
each increase. On each occasion, they reviewed both internal and external affordability data
before making the increase.
The first increase to £200 was made nine months after the account opened. Mr S was
managing the account well and making regular payments. His average balance was around
£35 and he had no borrowing on the account for three of the nine months. There was no
new adverse information from the CRA and so affordability appeared stable.
The limit then remained unchanged for around five years, until July 2023, when Studio
increased the limit to £400, after a request by Mr S. Mr S wasn’t using all the available credit
and his average balance was around £170. He was making regular payments, but there
were some occasions when these had been made late. But Mr S told Studio when he had
forgotten to make the payment and quickly resolved this. Mr S asked Studio to change the
repayment date until after his salary was paid, to stop this from happening. Once Studio had
done this, there weren’t any late payments afterwards. Late payments alone aren’t
necessarily a sign of financial difficulties, so I don’t think this would have been a reason for
Studio to decline further lending or carry out additional checks.
Overall, I believe the checks Studio carried out were proportionate. Considering the amount
being provided to Mr S, and the information Studio gathered, I don’t think they acted unfairly.
I say this because the limit was still modest, and although there were some signs of financial
difficulty in the past, everything in recent months had been much improved.
Studio increased the credit limit in October 2023 to £550 and again to £700 in December
when Mr S requested a further increase. The CRA data showed Mr S’ financial position was
stable. There were no arrears or negative indicators and his account with Studio was being
managed well. Mr S continued to make regular payments and did not rely on, or make use
of, all the additional credit. The maximum balance following both increases was around
£570.
In 2024, Studio increased the limit three more times, to its maximum of £1,000 in July.
Based on the information available to them at the time, Studio could see Mr S’ financial
circumstances remained consistent and there was nothing to suggest he was experiencing
financial difficulty or that further checks were required. He hadn’t used the additional credit to
its full extent and continued to make payments.
What matters is that the information remained broadly consistent. There was nothing to
suggest Mr S was having difficulty managing his borrowing. He made regular payments and
didn’t use the account to its limits. So, everything indicated he was managing the account
appropriately.
I’m not disputing that Mr S’ position may have been worse than it appeared or that he may
have been struggling. However, I don’t think this was evident to Studio either at the time they
gave him the account or increased his credit. And I think their checks went far enough, given
the repayment amounts and the positive management of Mr S’ account with them. So, it
follows that I think Studio made a fair decision to lend at the point of each increase too.
I’ve also carefully considered Mr S’ vulnerability and the impact this may have on his ability
to handle his financial commitments. I’m sorry to hear how difficult things have been for him,

and I appreciate how financial pressures can make things feel even harder. There’s nothing
to suggest this was brought to Studio’s attention before December 2025 or to show they
could have known earlier. So, I wouldn’t have expected the lender to have reasonably known
that Mr S was vulnerable, or to have taken any additional steps because of it.
Having reviewed all of the information provided, my view on the affordability of this account
remains unchanged, as there was nothing at the time of lending or the credit limit increases
to indicate to Studio that Mr S wasn’t appropriately managing his finances.
In reaching my conclusions, I’ve also considered whether the lending relationship between
Mr S and Studio might have been unfair to Mr S under s140A of the Consumer Credit Act
1974 (“CCA”). However, for the reasons I’ve already explained, I’m satisfied that Studio did
not lend irresponsibly when providing Mr S with this account, or by increasing his credit limit.
And I haven’t seen anything to suggest that s140A of the CCA would, given the facts of this
complaint, lead to a different outcome here.
While I appreciate this will be disappointing for Mr S, my final decision is that Studio did not
act unfairly when providing the credit account or by increasing the credit limit. So, I won’t be
upholding his complaint for the reasons I’ve explained above.
However, as Mr S has indicated he is struggling now, I remind Studio of its obligation to treat
him with forbearance.
My final decision
I don’t uphold this complaint against Frasers Group Financial Services Limited trading as
Studio.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr S to accept or
reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

Alison Wharton
Ombudsman

title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6337494 — Clarke Fencott LLP
text:
DRN-6337494

The complaint

Mr S complains about the advice given by Clarke Fencott LLP to transfer the benefits from
his defined-benefit (‘DB’) occupational pension scheme to a personal pension and retirement
annuity. He says the advice was unsuitable for him and believes this has caused a financial
loss.
What happened
The Investigator’s opinion, dated 9 April 2026, set out the full background to this complaint.
So I only intend to summarise what I consider key to my decision.

Mr S was an existing client of Clarke Fencott having previously received advice regarding his
pension arrangements in 2018. At that time, Mr S accessed funds from two personal
pensions in order to purchase a car. But Clarke Fencott had said that it couldn’t advise him
on his DB scheme, at that time, as Mr S was still an active member of the scheme.

Mr S approached Clarke Fencott again in 2021, having left his previous employer, to discuss
transferring his deferred DB scheme. The DB scheme had a cash equivalent transfer value
(‘CETV’) of £451,382.93.

Clarke Fencott completed a fact-find to gather information about Mr S’s circumstances and
objectives. Clarke Fencott also carried out an assessment of Mr S’s attitude to risk, which it
deemed to be ‘cautious’.

On 12 July 2021, Clarke Fencott advised Mr S to transfer his DB pension benefits into a
personal pension, taking full tax free cash (‘TFC’) and using £81,800 to purchase an annuity.
It advised that the remaining funds – a little under £245,000 - were invested in a drawdown
arrangement, in a managed portfolio in line with Mr S’s cautious attitude to risk.

The suitability report said the reasons for this recommendation were that it would enable
Mr S to take maximum TFC of £112,845.00, which he could use to purchase a property to
live in. This would, in turn, reduce his outgoings. The annuity would provide an income of
£3,500 per year, which added to his existing annuity and state pension when it became
payable, would provide a little under £13,500 per year. This would cover his core
expenditure. The remaining funds of just under £245,000 could then provide a flexible
income stream in retirement to top up Mr S’s income to the required £18,000. Mr S accepted
Clarke Fencott’s advice.

Mr S complained in 2025 to Clarke Fencott about the suitability of the transfer advice.

Clarke Fencott didn’t uphold Mr S’s complaint. In summary it said the recommendations had
been made in good faith. But it had no control over Mr S’s actions once he was in receipt of
the monies. It could only make a recommendation based on what Mr S presented to it in
terms of his situation, needs and objectives, and trust that those objectives are fulfilled.

Mr S referred his complaint to our service. An Investigator didn’t uphold the complaint. In
summary this was because he was satisfied the reasons for transferring Mr S’s DB pension

were made clear and were well documented. And alternative options applicable to Mr S’s
circumstances were considered by Clarke Fencott. So, the Investigator didn’t agree that
Clarke Fencott had failed to meet its regulatory obligations to Mr S. He thought Mr S had a
genuine objective that required access to a lump sum greater than he could achieve from the
DB scheme. And Clarke Fencott gave Mr S reasonable advice in respect of his income,
given his overall circumstances.

Mr S disagreed. In summary he said that:

•
Clarke Fencott’s own suitability report stated in explicit terms that the recommended
investment portfolio was “likely not achievable” in meeting the critical yield required to
justify the transfer.

•
Significant weight was placed on the property purchase objective as the justification
for the transfer. It’s not disputed that Mr S genuinely wanted to buy a home, and it’s
accepted the DB early retirement lump sum alone was insufficient for the properties
he had identified. However, Mr S didn’t purchase a property, he bought a caravan,
valued at £25,000. Paperwork from a review in 2024 states that Mr S was living with
his partner and approximately £43,845 of the funds intended for property purchase
had been used for other purposes.

•
The firm noted the total available for property purchase from the transfer and savings
was approximately £129,845. The highest-priced property Mr S identified was
£129,950. After Stamp Duty, conveyancing fees, survey costs, and basic removal
expenses, Mr S would have been left with virtually nothing in financial reserve.

•
Clarke Fencott’s own letter acknowledges the property was intended to give him
“security and peace of mind” at a time when he was very ill and had been forced from
his previous rental home. A recommendation that left him with zero buffer after the
purchase did not serve that objective.

•
The primary objective the transfer was said to be necessary to achieve – buying a
property -  was not achieved. That goes to the heart of whether the recommendation
was suitable.

•
Clarke Fencott’s income plan was constructed on the explicit basis that Mr S would
purchase a property, thereby eliminating his rental costs of £625 per month. His core
income requirement of £12,564 per year was calculated on the basis that he was no
longer paying rent. Mr S has not purchased a property but has continued to pay rent
throughout. His actual core income requirement therefore includes those rental costs.

•
Mr S was classified as a cautious investor. The DB scheme provided a guaranteed,
index-linked income of £10,413 per year, payable for life, with no investment risk, no
platform charges, and no dependence on market performance. The recommendation
placed Mr S into a flexible drawdown arrangement that was unlikely to achieve the
returns necessary to match what he was giving up.

•
Suitability is not simply a matter of reflecting back a client’s stated preferences. It
requires an objective assessment of the client’s capacity for loss.

•
Mr S has long Covid. At the time of the advice he had no certain prognosis and was
unable to claim benefits because his condition had not been diagnosed as
permanent.

•
The adjudication uses the health condition in one direction only — to reduce the
significance of what Mr S lost by transferring. It does not consider what the same
condition means for the appropriateness of the recommendation made. Mr S was
unwell, had no employment income, no prospect of returning to work, and no
meaningful assets beyond this pension. He was precisely the kind of client for whom
income certainty and capital protection should have been the absolute priority. The
guaranteed £10,413 per year from the DB scheme would have provided financial
security.

The Investigator wasn’t persuaded to change their opinion, so the complaint was referred to
me to make a final decision.

What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
I’ve taken into account relevant law and regulations, regulator’s rules, guidance and
standards and codes of practice, and what I consider to have been good industry practice at
the time. This includes the Principles for Business (PRIN) and the Conduct of Business
Sourcebook (‘COBS’). And where the evidence is incomplete, inconclusive or contradictory, I
reach my conclusions on the balance of probabilities – that is, what I think is more likely than
not to have happened based on the available evidence and the wider surrounding
circumstances.

I’d like to assure both parties that I’ve carefully considered everything provided. But while I
mean no discourtesy, I won’t address every point or piece of evidence provided. Instead, my
decision will focus on what I consider to be the key issues in reaching a fair and reasonable
outcome to this complaint.

The applicable rules, regulations and requirements

The below is not a comprehensive list of the rules and regulations which applied at the time
of the advice, but provides useful context for my assessment of Clarke Fencott's actions
here.

PRIN 6: A firm must pay due regard to the interests of its customers and treat them fairly.

PRIN 7: A firm must pay due regard to the information needs of its clients, and communicate
information to them in a way which is clear, fair and not misleading.

COBS 2.1.1R: A firm must act honestly, fairly and professionally in accordance with the best
interests of its client (the client's best interests rule).

The provisions in COBS 9 which deal with the obligations when giving a personal
recommendation and assessing suitability. And the provisions in COBS 19 which specifically
relate to a DB pension transfer.

Having considered all of this and the evidence in this case, I’ve decided not to uphold the
complaint for largely the same reasons given by the Investigator.

The regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority (‘FCA’), states in COBS 19.1.6G that the
starting assumption for a transfer from a DB scheme is that it is unsuitable. So, Clarke
Fencott should have only considered a transfer if it could clearly demonstrate, on

contemporary evidence, that the transfer was in Mr S’s best interests. And having looked at
all the evidence available, I’m satisfied it was in his best interests.

Financial viability

Clarke Fencott was required to carry out an appropriate transfer value analysis (‘APTA’) by
the regulator. This included producing a transfer value comparator (‘TVC’) – a comparison of
the CETV with the estimated monetary cost of acquiring the same benefits as those the DB
scheme guaranteed to provide at retirement. Clarke Fencott also calculated how much
Mr S’s pension fund would need to grow by each year in order to provide the same benefits
as his DB scheme (the critical yield). The suitability report referred to the contents of the
APTA.

For retiring at the normal DB scheme retirement age of 65, Clarke Fencott estimated that the
cost of replicating the DB scheme benefits was likely to be £910,003.50, which was over
£458,620 more than the CETV of Mr S’s DB scheme benefits. The critical yield was
estimated to be 13.91% per year to match the full pension that the DB scheme would
provide at 65 (starting at £18,597.66 per year). And to be 10.43% if Mr S took TFC and a
reduced pension.

Clarke Fencott also noted that Mr S was interested in taking his retirement benefits
immediately (at age 58). It said under the DB scheme rules early retirement factors would
apply. It explained that the critical yield for taking benefits immediately wasn’t relevant but
that it would cost £826,029.96 to obtain a comparable level of income to that provided by the
scheme at the age of 58. So £374,647.03 more than the CETV being offered by the DB
scheme.

It should be noted that the cost of replicating the DB scheme benefits included a spouse’s
and dependent pensions which, as I’ll come to, I’m satisfied Mr S didn’t need at that time.

The advice was given after the regulator gave instructions in Final Guidance FG17/9 as to
how businesses could calculate future 'discount rates' in loss assessments where a
complaint about a past pension transfer was being upheld. Prior to October 2017 similar
rates were published by the Financial Ombudsman Service on our website. Whilst
businesses weren't required to refer to these rates when giving advice on pension transfers,
they provide a useful indication of what growth rates would have been considered
reasonably achievable for a typical investor.

The relevant discount rates closest to when the advice was given which I can refer to was
published by the Financial Ombudsman Service for the period before 1 October 2017 and
was 3.3% per year for 6 years to retirement (age 65). I acknowledge that these were from
several years prior to the advice being given so I’ve also considered the regulator's standard
projection rates. The regulator's upper projection rate at the time of the advice was 8%, the
middle projection rate 5%, and the lower projection rate 2%.

I've taken all of this into account, along with the composition of assets in the discount rate,
Mr S’s ‘cautious’ attitude to risk. There would be little point in Mr S giving up the guarantees
available to him through his DB scheme only to achieve, at best, the same level of benefits
outside the scheme. But here I think Mr S was likely to receive benefits of a substantially
lower overall value than the DB scheme at retirement (at either age 58 or 65), as a result of
investing in line with that attitude to risk.

For this reason alone, I don’t think a transfer out of the DB scheme was in Mr S’s best
interests. Of course, financial viability isn’t the only consideration when giving transfer
advice, as Clarke Fencott has argued in this case. There might be other considerations

which mean a transfer is suitable, despite providing overall lower benefits. I’ve considered
this below.

Flexibility and income needs

The sales paperwork noted that Mr S had taken voluntary redundancy earlier in 2021. The
year before this he’d been seriously ill with Covid, requiring intensive care treatment in
hospital. And he was suffering from long Covid.  He’d been living off his redundancy
payment and an existing annuity, which provided an annual payment of £769. His total
expected expenditure in retirement equated to £20,064 per year, which included rent and a
minimal buffer of £40 per week.

The suitability report further noted that Mr S was currently renting but was looking to
purchase his own property to live in, to give him security and peace of mind. It noted that
Mr S had provided details of properties he was interested in purchasing, ranging between
£100,000 and £130,000.

Clarke Fencott wasn’t just there to enable Mr S to meet his objectives; a firm’s role isn’t
simply to facilitate whatever course of action a consumer wants to take. The firm has a
regulatory responsibility to look at things objectively and to provide suitable advice based on
what it considers to be in the consumer’s best interests. It’s therefore important to note that
what a consumer might want to do or what they think is best for them might not align with
what a firm considers to be suitable or in their best interests. This is because the consumer’s
objectives or wishes might be unrealistic and/or impossible to achieve in the circumstances.
Or there might be alternative, lower risk options available to meet the consumer’s objectives
such that it would be unsuitable to relinquish valuable benefit guarantees.

In this case, I can understand why buying his own property was important to Mr S,
particularly as he’d had to move out of his rented accommodation the year before, while
suffering from long Covid. I don’t think purchasing a property would have been achieved by
staying in the DB scheme. The TFC available under the DB scheme, with his existing
savings and remaining redundancy money, would not have been sufficient to enable him to
purchase a property. However, the TFC available if Mr S took the CETV lump sum on offer,
would be sufficient, and there was the possibility to top this up with his existing savings and
his remaining redundancy payment. The suitability report went on to explain that this in turn
would reduce Mr S’s monthly outgoing by £650 as he wouldn’t be paying rent.

Mr S has acknowledged that he wanted to buy a property but he has said that even if the
transfer provided him with sufficient funds to purchase a property, this left him with no buffer
to pay the additional costs involved in the purchase, such as conveyancing fees and stamp
duty.

I think it’s worth noting that, as a first time buyer, it’s unlikely Mr S would have been required
to pay stamp duty as the properties he was considering were below the stamp duty
threshold. And while purchasing the most expensive property he’d been considering would
have left very little to cover any additional fees, Mr S had also been considering less
expensive properties. Further, Mr S had access to significant funds in his drawdown plan,
should he have found himself having insufficient funds to complete the purchase. So I think
the advice put Mr S in a position where it would have possible to purchase a property. The
fact that he didn’t go on to do this doesn’t mean the advice was unsuitable at the time. I think
the advice gave Mr S the flexibility he required in order to meet his objective of purchasing
somewhere to live.

The advice to use some of the remaining funds to purchase an annuity, and top up his
income until he reached state retirement age using the funds remaining in drawdown, would

have enabled Mr S to meet his expected expenditure. He would then be able to reduce the
amount he was drawing down accordingly once his state pension came into payment at age
67.

Other than his minimal annuity, Mr S had no other income at the time of advice. He was
living off his savings and redundancy payment and I’ve not seen that Mr S had a prospect of
any further income at that time, in fact the sales paperwork noted that he considered himelf
retired. And based on his expected expenditure, these funds would only last around a year.
So Mr S needed access to funds, either through the DB scheme or by transferring and
accessing the CETV.  As I’ve said above the TFC available from the scheme wasn’t
sufficient to have enabled him to purchase a property. And taking benefits from the DB
scheme early wouldn’t have given him sufficient income to cover his core expenditure,
including rent.  So I think buying a property was a reasonable objective.

Overall, I think Mr S had a strong need for an increased TFC lump sum and variable income
throughout his retirement. Transferring his DB pension gave him both of these and would
have enabled him to purchase a property, thereby reducing his income needs by around
£7,500 per year.

Mr S’s cautious attitude to risk

I accept that Mr S was deemed to have a cautious attitude to risk but I think the opportunity
of purchasing his own home would have been appealing and would have given him security
and peace of mind. I accept that generally, a cautious investor would want to avoid giving up
the guaranteed income the DB scheme provided. But I think Clarke Fencott took this into
account by recommending a blended approach of some guaranteed pension (through the
purchase of an annuity) and the remainder exposed to investment risk. I think this was a
suitable recommendation in Mr S’s particular circumstances. This option provided some
guarantees while providing Mr S with the means to purchase a property and generate
sufficient income to cover his expected expenditure.

Death benefits

The sales paperwork said that Mr S was single with no dependent children. I know Mr S has
since said that he is living with a partner. However, I’m persuaded the sales paperwork
provided an accurate picture of his circumstances, at the time of advice. So I think it was
reasonable for the adviser to have assumed that Mr S didn’t have any need for the spouse’s
or dependent’s pension that the DB scheme provided. As such, I don’t think losing these
benefits disadvantaged Mr S. And I think he preferred the ability to pass on whatever
remained of his pension to a beneficiary of his choice on his death.

Conclusion

Overall, although I accept that Mr S was unlikely to achieve the critical yield required to
match the scheme benefits at retirement, I think there were other reasons that meant the
advice to transfer was suitable. So, for the above reasons, I don’t think Clarke Fencott acted
unfairly or unreasonably.

My final decision
For the reason explained, I don’t uphold this complaint.

Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr S to accept or
reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

Lorna Goulding

Ombudsman

title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6390098 — Clydesdale Financial Services Limited
text:
DRN-6390098

The complaint

Mrs S’s complaint is, in essence, that Clydesdale Financial Services Limited, trading as
Barclays Partner Finance (the ‘Lender’) acted unfairly and unreasonably by (1) being party to
an unfair credit relationship with her under Section 140A of the Consumer Credit Act 1974
(as amended) (the ‘CCA’) and (2) deciding against paying a claim under Section 75 of the
CCA.

Mrs S is represented in her complaint by a professional representative (“PR”).

What happened
I issued a provisional decision on Mrs S’s complaint on 22 August 2025, in which I set out
the background to this matter, and my provisional findings on the concerns set out. A copy of
that provisional decision is appended to, and forms part of, this final decision, so it’s not
necessary for me to go over the details again. But to summarise briefly:
•
Mrs S had been a long-term member of a timeshare provider (the “Supplier”), having
made a number of purchases from it over the years. However, her complaint
concerned a purchase she’d made from the Supplier with finance from the Lender,
on 27 September 2013.
•
The purchase in question involved buying 16,000 points in the Supplier’s “Fractional
Club”, paying £10,235 and trading in 15,000 points she already had in the Supplier’s
“European Collection” – a different timeshare club. Both clubs worked in a similar
way, with the main differences being that the Fractional Club had a shorter
membership term (15 years) and entitled Mrs S to a share in the net sale proceeds of
a named property (the “Allocated Property”) at the end of the membership. £7,325 of
the purchase price was financed by a loan with the Lender, arranged by the Supplier
(the “Credit Agreement”).
•
Via PR, Mrs S complained to the Lender on 12 June 2017 about a number of
different mis-selling concerns regarding the timeshare and the associated Credit
Agreement. Mrs S sought to find the Lender responsible for these concerns under
the principles of connected lender liability – more specifically Sections 75 and 140A
of the CCA. The Lender rejected the complaint, which was then referred to the
Financial Ombudsman Service.
In my provisional decision, I said I didn’t think the complaint should be upheld. The full
reasons can be found in the appended document, but again I will summarise:
•
I considered there was insufficient persuasive evidence the Supplier had falsely
represented to Mrs S that buying Fractional Club membership was the only way to
get out of her European Collection membership, or that the new membership came
with a specific guaranteed exit date. I also considered some of the allegations made
were rather vague, which made it difficult to establish that a specific false statement
had been made to Mrs S.

•
Regarding alleged breaches of contract by the Supplier, I was satisfied that the
contractual arrangements gave her an interest in the Allocated Property which
entitled her to receive a proportionate share in its net sale proceeds. I considered any
breaches of contract lay potentially in the future, but there was no breach of contract
currently. Complaints about other alleged breaches concerning the availability and
price of holidays, I considered were insufficiently evidenced to succeed.
•
PR had set out a variety of concerns which appeared to be matters which it was
saying rendered Mrs S’s credit relationship with the Lender unfair to her. I didn’t think
these concerns had led to an unfair credit relationship because:
o There was little evidence to support a contention that Mrs S had been
pressured into making the purchase, and she had also not used her cooling
off period to cancel, which might have been expected had she felt pressured
to sign up on the day.
o Whether or not the Lender had carried out the kind of affordability checks it
should have done, evidence had not been offered of the loan having been
unaffordable.
o Similarly, whether or not the Supplier had provided sufficient information
about the ongoing costs of the timeshare, or had incorporated unfair terms in
its contract with Mrs S, I had not seen evidence that these alleged wrongs
had led to significant harm or unfairness affecting Mrs S in practice.
•
Due to the importance which was later attached to a specific allegation – that the
Supplier had sold or marketed the timeshare to Mrs S as an investment, in breach of
the regulations on selling timeshares – I considered this point in further detail, finding
that any breach by the Supplier of the regulations had probably not influenced
Mrs S’s purchasing decision in a material way. Specifically:
o I found the fact that this allegation had not featured in Mrs S’s original
complaint in 2017, and had only been made some seven years later,
suggested it had not been an important factor in her decision making (if it had
happened).
o I noted certain disclaimers Mrs S had signed at the time of making the
purchase, which declared that the product was not to be regarded as an
investment, and thought these suggested the Supplier had taken some steps
to avoid selling the product as an investment, and/or that Mrs S may have
understood that the product was not an investment.
o I found it difficult to rely on a witness statement PR had submitted later in
2023, in which Mrs S recalled the timeshare having been sold as an
investment and this being a key reason why she’d bought it. PR said it had
received the witness statement in early 2017, but I thought there was
evidence which called that claim into question and it was possible the
statement had been produced at a later date.
At the time of writing the provisional decision, I didn’t have sufficient information to be able to
make any findings on another concern raised by PR, which was that the Lender had
allegedly paid an undisclosed commission to the Supplier for arranging the Credit
Agreement.
I invited the parties to let me have any further submissions they wanted me to consider while

the matter of commission was investigated further. The Lender said it accepted the
provisional decision. PR said it disagreed and sent in extensive submissions. These were
later withdrawn and replaced by a more concise set of submissions along with various
supporting documents. I could summarise PR’s arguments as follows:
•
The witness statement was a genuine document from 2017 and the fact it had not
been submitted at the time the complaint was referred to the Financial Ombudsman
Service was because a senior figure at the Financial Ombudsman Service had
instructed PR not to do so in a letter dating to April 2018. PR was therefore unhappy
the witness statement had not been given more weight.
•
A questionnaire Mrs S had also completed in 2017, supported the account of events
she gave in her witness statement. When asked if she had been guaranteed a profit
by the Supplier, she had answered that she had been.
•
While it may have been the case that the original complaint letter didn’t mention the
timeshare was sold as an investment, the factual matrix demonstrated that it was.
The letter articulated that Mrs S was promised a share in property and a subsequent
return from the sale of the asset. Outlaying money for a share in an asset with the
expectation of receiving proceeds upon its sale constitutes the fundamental
mechanism of an investment. The letter also referred to it being a breach of contract
that Mrs S wouldn’t receive the net sale proceeds as she didn’t have confirmation
that she owned any part of the property.
•
The original letter of complaint argued that Mrs S was advised she would be
guaranteed an exit from her membership in a certain number of years, but this was
untrue as the scheme could only be brought to an end if a purchaser was found. The
fact that this concern had featured in the original complaint was evidence that the
matter of investment had been complained about in 2017.
•
It was unsafe for me to rely only on the disclaimers in the Supplier’s paperwork, in
line with what the relevant case law had to say about reliance on such disclaimers.
•
Mrs S’s decision to buy the timeshare made no sense unless she was expecting a
profitable financial return at the end. It could not have been bought for holidays as it
was so expensive.
Having received further information on the question of commission, I then issued a letter to
the parties in which I observed that no commission had been paid and I saw no reason why
Mrs S’s complaint should be upheld because of the commission arrangements between the
Lender and the Supplier.
Following a challenge by PR, I made further enquiries and it became apparent the Lender
had initially provided inaccurate information – and a commission of £590.38 – or 8.16% of
the loan amount – had been paid to the Supplier.
I didn’t think, however, that a commission at this level was enough by itself to have rendered
Mrs S’s credit relationship with he Lender unfair to her. Further, I noted I hadn’t seen
anything to suggest that the Lender and Supplier were tied to one another contractually or
commercially in a way that wasn’t properly disclosed to Mrs S. Nor had I seen anything that
persuaded me that the commission arrangement between them gave the Supplier a choice
over the interest rate that led Mrs S into a credit agreement that cost disproportionately more
than it otherwise could have.
PR proclaimed its dissatisfaction with this answer and with how the Lender had conducted

itself. In essence, it argued that the Lender had not been candid and it was now essential to
see the actual commercial agreements between the Lender and Supplier which applied at
the relevant time, as there could be aspects of this agreement which rendered Mrs S’s credit
relationship with the Lender unfair to her. PR noted that the burden of proof lay with the
Lender to show that the credit relationship had not been rendered unfair.
The case has now been returned to me to review once more.
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Having done so, I’ve arrived at essentially the same set of conclusions as in my appended
provisional decision, and for much the same reasons. I don’t propose to go over points which
have not been disputed following the provisional decision and I will focus only on the matters
which have been argued by PR in response – namely the matter of the Supplier’s alleged
breach of Regulation 14(3) of the Timeshare Regulations, and the payment of a commission
by the Lender to the Supplier, and the impact of these on the fairness of the credit
relationship.
I think it’s important to make the point that, in contrast to what might happen in court, neither
side to this complaint has a burden of proof that it must discharge. After all, the jurisdiction
under which I’m deciding this complaint is inquisitorial rather than adversarial – which means
that my findings are made, on the balance of probabilities, in light of the evidence and/or
arguments from both sides.

So, while PR argues in response to my provisional decision that, under Section 140B of the
CCA, it is for the Lender to prove that its credit relationship with Mrs S wasn’t unfair simply
because she alleges that it was, that fails to understand that the Financial Ombudsman
Service deals with complaints rather than causes of action. And, in any event, to suggest
that unsubstantiated allegations of fact must be disproved by the Lender if the credit
relationship isn’t to be deemed unfair also oversimplifies if not misunderstands the legal
position. As HHJ David Cooke said in paragraph 26 of his judgment on Promontoria
(Henrico) Ltd v. Gurcharn Samra [2019] EWHC 2327 (Ch):

“…the onus is on [the creditor] to show, to the normal civil standard, that the relationship is
not unfair because of any of the reasons set out in s 140A(1)(a)-(c). Whether it is so unfair is
a matter for the court's overall judgment having regard to all the relevant circumstances and
matters, including matters relating (i.e. personal) to the creditor and debtor. This onus on the
claimant does not however mean, in my judgement…that where [the borrower alleging an
unfair credit relationship] makes allegations of fact on which he relies he does not have the
burden of proving them to the normal civil standard. The onus placed on the creditor is as to
the relationship between it and the debtor, and does not have the effect that factual
allegations made by Mr Samra must be accepted unless they can be positively disproved by
contrary evidence.”1

The alleged breach of Regulation 14(3) of the Timeshare Regulations

I thank PR for its further submissions. Unfortunately, I feel these undermine rather than
support its central allegation that the Supplier marketed or sold the timeshare as an
investment when Mrs S bought it, or that any such marketing was influential in her decision-
making process at the time. I’ll explain why.

1 As approved by the Supreme Court in Smith v. The Royal Bank of Scotland plc [2023] UKSC 34 – see paragraph 40.

Firstly, I can’t see how a letter PR received from the Financial Ombudsman Service in April
2018 could have prevented it from sending us Mrs S’s witness statement in October 2017
when it referred the complaint to us. This clearly can’t be correct.
Secondly, a key piece of evidence relied on in PR’s recent submissions is a questionnaire
completed by Mrs S in August 2017 – some months after the witness statement PR said it
had received from Mrs S in February 2017. PR says that in this document, Mrs S said she’d
been guaranteed a profit by the Supplier. This isn’t the case.
I’ve reviewed the questionnaire, which covers multiple purchases from the Supplier. When
Mrs S was asked, of the September 2013 purchase, if the Supplier had guaranteed a profit
at the end of her membership, she did not answer this question. She didn’t tick either the
“Yes” or “No” boxes. There was then a question which asked her, if she had answered “Yes”
to the previous question, to indicate what profit she had been told she would make. This was
also left blank.
So Mrs S didn’t indicate that she’d been guaranteed a profit in the questionnaire.
Mrs S made various comments in free text boxes when completing the questionnaire. From
these, it is apparent that she didn’t purchase the timeshare because she thought it was an
investment. She said that the purpose of the purchase had been to:
“…have my points converted into a share of a property and to sell my share as a way out of
not having to pay maintenance fees until I die!”
And
“To eventually get rid of the timeshare and have no maintenance fees to pay!”
Later in the questionnaire, Mrs S was asked to provide any further information which she
believed may be of note. She said:
“The reason for fractioning my points was to have an end in sight for maintenance payments
to cease and sell my share of the property. No doubt [Supplier] would come up with some
excuse or “wonderful plan” to get yet more money out of members. On a visit to Pine Lake I
was given a verbal valuation on my share of the property of £32,000!!! Ha! Ha! I do not
remember any mention or signing anything to do with timeshare being in perpetuity.”
While Mrs S recalls the Supplier telling her that her share was worth much more than she
paid for it – this appears to have been some time after the purchase, at a different resort, so
it could not have influenced her decision to buy it. It also doesn’t appear from Mrs S’s
reaction to being told how much the share was worth, that she believed what she was told.
I don’t think Mrs S’s answers to the questionnaire are consistent with the (apparently earlier)
witness statement. She doesn’t say a profit was guaranteed despite being asked about this,
and makes no mention of either being told that the product was an investment, or of
believing that to be the case. In fact, her comments suggest she was sceptical of later
apparently optimistic valuations given to her by the Supplier.
I would also note that the February 2017 witness statement is written in a different style to
Mrs S’s other written submissions. There is much more character, colour and detail in her
responses to the questionnaire. The witness statement is brief and dry in style, and lacks the
emotional expression that appears in the questionnaire responses. I remain of the view that
its provenance must be considered uncertain – I’m not confident that it was produced in or
around February 2017 and I can not place any weight on it.

I’ve considered PR’s other points regarding the alleged sale of the timeshare to Mrs S as an
investment, but I do not find them persuasive. I can’t see that any amount of reinterpretation
of the original letter of complaint can lead me to a conclusion that it contained an allegation
that the timeshare was sold to Mrs S as an investment. This leaves me with the following key
findings:
•
In the original letter of complaint, there was no allegation that the Supplier sold the
timeshare to Mrs S as an investment.
•
In Mrs S’s 2017 questionnaire, she didn’t identify the Supplier as having sold the
timeshare to her as an investment or having told her that she’d make a profit. She
also didn’t mention making the purchase because she thought it was an investment,
instead identifying other reasons.
•
The allegation that the timeshare was sold as an investment appeared only later in
2023, after developments in the courts had made it apparent that the sale of a
timeshare as an investment was something that might very well render a credit
relationship with a connected lender, unfair to the borrower.
In light of this, I don’t think it’s likely the Supplier marketed or sold the timeshare to Mrs S in
September 2013 as an investment. And even if it did, it’s apparent this didn’t have a material
impact on her purchasing decision, as she bought the timeshare for other reasons.
The matter of the commission payment by the Lender to the Supplier
It’s unfortunate that the Lender didn’t initially provide accurate information about the
commission payment to the Supplier in Mrs S’s case. As I mentioned above, the actual
amount was £590.38, equal to 8.16% of the loan amount.
To ensure the reasoning in this decision is complete (given this point was not covered in the
appended provisional decision), I will address it in full here.
PR says that a payment of commission from the Lender to the Supplier at the Time of Sale
should lead me to uphold this complaint because, simply put, information in relation to that
payment went undisclosed at the Time of Sale.
As both sides already know, the Supreme Court handed down an important judgment on 1
August 2025 in a series of cases concerned with the issue of commission: Johnson v
FirstRand Bank Ltd, Wrench v FirstRand Bank Ltd and Hopcraft v Close Brothers Ltd [2025]
UKSC 33 (‘Hopcraft, Johnson and Wrench’).
The Supreme Court ruled that, in each of the three cases, the commission payments made
to car dealers by lenders were legal, as claims for the tort of bribery, or the dishonest
assistance of a breach of fiduciary duty, had to be predicated on the car dealer owing a
fiduciary duty to the consumer, which the car dealers did not owe. A “disinterested duty”, as
described in Wood v Commercial First Business Ltd & ors and Business Mortgage Finance 4
plc v Pengelly [2021] EWCA Civ 471, is not enough.
However, the Supreme Court held that the credit relationship between the lender and Mr
Johnson was unfair under Section 140A of the CCA because of the commission paid by the
lender to the car dealer. The main reasons for coming to that conclusion included, amongst
other things, the following factors:

1. The size of the commission (as a percentage of the total charge for credit). In Mr
Johnson’s case it was 55%. This was “so high” and “a powerful indication that the
relationship…was unfair” (see paragraph 327);
2. The failure to disclose the commission; and
3. The concealment of the commercial tie between the car dealer and the lender.
The Supreme Court also confirmed that the following factors, in what was a non-exhaustive
list, will normally be relevant when assessing whether a credit relationship was/is unfair
under Section 140A of the CCA:
1. The size of the commission as a proportion of the charge for credit;
2. The way in which commission is calculated (a discretionary commission arrangement, for
example, may lead to higher interest rates);
3. The characteristics of the consumer;
4. The extent of any disclosure and the manner of that disclosure (which, insofar as
Section 56 of the CCA is engaged, includes any disclosure by a supplier when acting as
a broker); and
5. Compliance with the regulatory rules.
From my reading of the Supreme Court’s judgment in Hopcraft, Johnson and Wrench, it sets
out principles which apply to credit brokers other than car dealer–credit brokers. So, when
considering allegations of undisclosed payments of commission like the one in this
complaint, Hopcraft, Johnson and Wrench is relevant law that I’m required to consider under
Rule 3.6.4 of the Financial Conduct Authority’s Dispute Resolution Rules (‘DISP’).
But I don’t think Hopcraft, Johnson and Wrench assists Mrs S in arguing that her credit
relationship with the Lender was unfair to her for reasons relating to commission given the
facts and circumstances of this complaint.
PR has – in light of the Lender’s failure to provide the correct commission details initially –
indicated that a more thorough investigation into the Lender’s commercial agreements with
the Supplier is necessary. It has asked whether we have requested a copy of the
commercial agreement.
In my most recent update to PR, I said:
“I can confirm that we have investigated with [the Lender], as we have with other lenders, the
nature of their commission arrangements with timeshare providers. As you are aware, under
DISP 3.5.9(2)R we are able to provide an edited version, description or summary of
information which has been received in confidence and is commercially sensitive.
This is applicable to the results of our investigations with [the Lender].”
I can confirm to PR that we did request a copy of the commercial agreement as part of our
investigations. The Lender informed us that it no longer has a record of the commercial
agreement which covers this loan. This is unfortunate, though perhaps not unexpected or
unreasonable given the length of time that has passed since the Time of Sale.

Ultimately, I have to make a decision on the balance of probabilities, even where I don’t have
all the evidence or information I would have liked to have seen. And it remains the case that
I haven’t seen anything to suggest that the Lender and Supplier were tied to one another
contractually or commercially in a way that wasn’t properly disclosed to Mrs S, nor have I
seen anything that persuades me that the commission arrangement between them gave the
Supplier a choice over the interest rate that led Mrs S into a credit agreement that cost
disproportionately more than it otherwise could have.
I acknowledge that it’s possible that the Lender and the Supplier failed to follow the
regulatory guidance in place at the Time of Sale insofar as it was relevant to disclosing the
commission arrangements between them.
But as I’ve said before, the case law on Section 140A makes it clear that regulatory
breaches do not automatically create unfairness for the purposes of that provision. Such
breaches and their consequences (if there are any) must be considered in the round, rather
than in a narrow or technical way. And with that being the case, it isn’t necessary to make a
formal finding on that because, even if the Lender and the Supplier failed to follow the
relevant regulatory guidance at the Time of Sale, it is for the reasons set out below that I
don’t currently think any such failure is itself a reason to find the credit relationship in
question unfair to Mrs S.
In stark contrast to the facts of Mr Johnson’s case, the amount of commission paid by the
Lender to the Supplier for arranging the Credit Agreement that [Consumer] entered into
wasn’t high. At £590.38, it was only 8.16% of the amount borrowed. So, had she known at
the Time of Sale that the Supplier was going to be paid a flat rate of commission at that
level, I’m not currently persuaded that she either wouldn’t have understood that or would
have otherwise questioned the size of the payment at that time. After all, at the time it seems
Mrs S wanted to switch to Fractional Club membership and had no obvious means of her
own to pay for it. And at such a low level, the impact of commission on the cost of the credit
she needed for a product she wanted doesn’t strike me as disproportionate. So, I think she
would still have taken out the loan to fund her purchase at the Time of Sale had the amount
of commission been disclosed.
What’s more, based on what I’ve seen so far, the Supplier’s role as a credit broker wasn’t a
separate service and distinct from its role as the seller of timeshares. It was simply a means
to an end in the Supplier’s overall pursuit of a successful timeshare sale. I can’t see that the
Supplier gave an undertaking – either expressly or impliedly – to put to one side its
commercial interests in pursuit of that goal when arranging the Credit Agreement. And as it
wasn’t acting as an agent of Mrs S but as the supplier of contractual rights she obtained
under the Purchase Agreement, the transaction doesn’t strike me as one with features that
suggest the Supplier had an obligation of ‘loyalty’ to her when arranging the Credit
Agreement and thus a fiduciary duty.
Overall, therefore, I’m not currently persuaded that the commission arrangements between
the Supplier and the Lender were likely to have led to a sufficiently extreme inequality of
knowledge that rendered the credit relationship unfair to Mrs S.
Section 140A: Conclusion
Given all of the factors I’ve looked at in this part of my decision, and having taken all of them
into account, I’m not persuaded that the credit relationship between Mrs S and the Lender
under the Credit Agreement and related Purchase Agreement was unfair to her. And as
things currently stand, I don’t think it would be fair or reasonable that I uphold this complaint
on that basis.

Commission: The Alternative Grounds of Complaint
While I’ve found that Mrs S’s credit relationship with the Lender wasn’t unfair to her for
reasons relating to the commission arrangements between it and the Supplier, two of the
grounds on which I came to that conclusion also constitute separate and freestanding
complaints to Mrs S’s complaint about an unfair credit relationship. So, for completeness,
I’ve considered those grounds on that basis here.
The first ground relates to whether the Lender is liable for the dishonest assistance of a
breach of fiduciary duty by the Supplier because it took a payment of commission from the
Lender without telling Mrs S (i.e., secretly). And the second relates to the Lender’s
compliance with the regulatory guidance in place at the Time of Sale insofar as it was
relevant to disclosing the commission arrangements between them.
However, for the reasons I set out above, I’m not persuaded that the Supplier – when acting
as credit broker – owed Mrs S a fiduciary duty. So, the remedies that might be available at
law in relation to the payment of secret commission aren’t, in my view, available to her. And
while it’s possible that the Lender failed to follow the regulatory guidance in place at the
Time of Sale insofar as it was relevant to disclosing the commission arrangements between
it and the Supplier, I don’t think any such failure on the Lender’s part is itself a reason to
uphold this complaint because, for the reasons I also set out above, I think she would still
have taken out the loan to fund her purchase at the Time of Sale had there been more
adequate disclosure of the commission arrangements that applied at that time.
My final decision
