The reasons why I’ve been unable to conclude any potential marketing by the Supplier of the
Fractional Club product to Mrs S as an investment is likely to have had a material impact on
her decision to make her purchase, are primarily based on difficulties I have with the
evidence. I’ll explain why.

The PR did not originally allege that the Supplier had sold or marketed the product in
this way

The Letter of Complaint made no mention of the Supplier having marketed or sold the
Fractional Club membership to Mrs S as an investment. This allegation was first made by
the PR almost seven years after the complaint was originally brought to the Lender. In light
of this it seems unlikely to me that – even if the Supplier did market the product in this way –
this was a material factor in Mrs S’s purchasing decision. If it was significant I would have
expected it to have featured prominently in these initial submissions.

Mrs S appears to have ticked and signed to say she understood the product was not
an investment

Mrs S signed a declaration at the Time of Sale, and ticked against a statement on this
declaration which said: “We understand that…[the product] should not be regarded as a
property or financial investment.” While what is committed to writing doesn’t always reflect
what was said verbally, this indicates to me that a) the Supplier made some efforts not to
market or sell the product to Mrs S as an investment, and b) Mrs S may have understood
that the product was not an investment. If she did, it would be difficult to conclude this was a
material reason for her having bought it.

It is not possible to place weight on the witness statement said to have been written
by Mrs S in 2017

I’ve seen a copy of an undated and unsigned witness statement which the PR says it
received from Mrs S in February 2017. It says it received this as part of a pack of documents
from Mrs S, and that it was sending us the pack because another document within the pack
was dated to show when it was received. And indeed, the second document in the pack has
been stamped with “Received 15 Feb 2017”. The witness statement is short and focuses
very clearly on the Supplier having sold the product to Mrs S as an investment, and this
being the reason why she was convinced to make the purchase. The only other concerns
expressed in the witness statement which are consistent with the Letter of Complaint are a
passing reference to having been pressured into making the purchase, and a desire to avoid
paying ongoing costs in future. Given how much focus Mrs S gives to the matter of the
product having been sold to her as an investment in this witness statement, I am surprised
that this did not feature at all in the Letter of Complaint.

It’s also worth noting that we received a different pack from the PR in October 2017
containing the same document which had been stamped as having been received on 15
February 2017, but without this stamp on it. It seems odd that a document stamped to record
its receipt on 15 February 2017, could be sent to the Financial Ombudsman Service some
months later missing this stamp. While there could be an innocent explanation for this
discrepancy, in my mind this calls into question the provenance of the witness statement.
Given this questionable provenance, lack of consistency with the complaint as originally
made, and its very late emergence as a piece of evidence, I am able to place only the most
limited amount of weight on it. I do not find it persuasive.

Overall, I think there’s a lack of evidence to support an argument that any improper
marketing of the Fractional Club membership to Mrs S by the Supplier, had a material impact
on her decision to go ahead with the purchase.

Mrs S’s Commission Complaint

One of Mrs S other concerns relates to alleged payments of commission by the Lender to
the Supplier for acting as a credit broker and arranging the Credit Agreement. The Supreme
Court’s recent judgment Johnson v FirstRand Bank Ltd, Wrench v FirstRand Bank Ltd and
Hopcroft v Close Brothers Ltd [2025] UKSC 33 (‘Johnson, Wrench and Hopcroft’) clarified
the law on payments of commission – albeit in the context of car dealers acting as credit
brokers. In my view, the Supreme Court’s judgment sets out principles which appear capable
of applying to credit brokers other than car dealer–credit brokers. At present, I do not know
what, if any, commission was paid by the Lender in relation to the Credit Agreement. So,
once I know more, I will finalise my findings on this complaint.

Conclusion

In conclusion, as things currently stand, I do not think that the Lender acted unfairly or
unreasonably when it dealt with the relevant Section 75 claim, and if I put the issue of
commission to one side for the time being, I am not persuaded that the Lender was party to
a credit relationship with Mrs S under the Credit Agreements that was unfair to her for the
purposes of Section 140A of the CCA – nor do I see any other reason why it would be fair or
reasonable to direct the Lender to compensate her.

But, as I’ve already said, I do not know what, if any, commission was paid by the Lender in
relation to the Credit Agreement. And with that being the case, it is necessary to wait for that
information before finalising my thoughts on the merits of this complaint.

My provisional decision
For the reasons explained above, I’m not currently minded to uphold this complaint, but need
to wait until further information is known about the matter of any commission paid by the
Lender in relation to the Credit Agreement.

Will Culley
Ombudsman

title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6340068 — Curtis Banks Limited
text:
DRN-6340068

The complaint

Mr E complains that Curtis Banks Limited (‘Curtis Banks’) delayed the transfer of his pension
monies from an investment platform back to his Self-invested Personal Pension (‘SIPP’) and
then on to a different third-party business for a foreign currency trade. Mr E says that he
missed out on interest and suffered significant distress and inconvenience because of the
delay.

What happened
Mr E had a SIPP with Curtis Banks and monies within it were held with a third-party
investment platform that I’ll refer to as Provider T. In March 2025, Mr E – or his adviser on
his behalf – instructed Curtis Banks to withdraw the funds held with Provider T. This was to
enable Mr E to place a foreign currency trade via another third-party business that I’ll refer to
as Business H.

Mr E’s adviser instructed the withdrawal on 5 March 2025, and he has told us that the
transaction didn’t complete until 2 June 2025.

Prior to and throughout the time it took to process the transaction Mr E has complained
about here, similar transactions involving the same businesses – but involving different
investors – were being processed. And some of these other transactions involved similar
issues to those experienced by Mr E.

We’ve been provided with submissions by the parties to the complaint including email chains
and secure messages exchanged between the various parties involved in the transaction.
These relate to Mr E’s transaction, other relevant transactions going on at the same time and
some of the wider conversations ongoing between the regulated parties involved.

I’ve set out some of the correspondence and relevant dates below.

Timeline of key events:

5 March 2025 – Mr E’s adviser notified Curtis Banks that it had instructed Provider T to
disinvest his portfolio and instructed Curtis Banks to arrange for the funds to be remitted
back to the SIPP.

7 March 2025 – The adviser followed up to confirm that the funds were now (then) in cash
and request an update.

11 March 2025 – Curtis Banks responded confirming that the request for the funds had been
sent the day before (10 March 2025).

On the same day Provider T responded to the request, it said:

“Further to the withdrawal request we have received on the above portfolio, in order
to proceed we will require:

The sig list refers to a PoA document dated 13/08/24 and a board resolution dated
30/01/24, please can we have a copy of these.

Please can all documents be certified, I attach our guide for reference

Once we have the above our legal team will re-review. Please note, after this, there
may be additional requirements.”

Curtis Banks responded, again on the same day, attaching the documents. Provider T
confirmed that the documents had to be uploaded or posted and noting that only one of the
documents was certified but they required each document to be certified.

12 March 2025 – Curtis Banks sent an email attaching the relevant documents and
confirming that these had been sent by post as well.

19 March 2025 – the adviser followed up again, confirming that it had spoken to Provider T
and it had been told that:

“I can confirm that we have received the instruction and are currently trying to resolve
the closure.

We require a signatory list, along with the mentioned legal documentation that the
signature list refers to.

[Curtis Banks] confirmed these have been posted to us on 12th but we are yet to
receive.”

The adviser queried whether these documents could be sent via secure message or if they
had to be posted.

Curtis Banks responded on the same day and confirmed that:

“We are currently working on this, as I did email [Provider T] the document I was
planning to post them and they informed me that it wouldn’t meet the requirements
for the disinvestment to take place, so I didn’t post these.

We are looking into how to get the required documents over to [Provider T] to allow
this to be actioned.”

20 March 2025 – the adviser responded confirming the urgency of the transfer being
actioned and that it could upload any necessary documents to Provider T’s system if Curtis
Banks sent them to it by email. The adviser also highlighted that:

“From my understanding there were a number of issues with [Provider T] at the very
start of the year…We understood that these were all resolved and Curtis Banks and
[Provider T] had a clear agreed process to move forward with.”

The documents were sent to Mr E’s adviser and uploaded to the portal (it doesn’t appear
that Curtis Banks had access to this) on the same day.

Following this, both Curtis Banks and the adviser chased Provider T for updates.

31 March 2025 – the adviser confirmed that, having followed up with Provider T, it had been
told that the document sent the week before was not the correct one:

“… [Provider T] require the Principal Powers of Attorney document - as the one CB
have sent is the Delegation Powers of Attorney and this is not the one they need.

Please can you urgently review this and sent [sic] the correct one. I can confirm that
[Provider T] require either the original or a certified copy of the Principal POA doc - if
possible please can this also be sent to us directly as well and we can upload it via
our platform.”

This was followed up on a number of occasions with the adviser highlighting, amongst other
things, that in another case the necessary paperwork had been issued within a couple of
days, so it wasn’t clear what the hold up was here.

1 April 2025 – Curtis Banks placed the trade with Business H, this set out that:

“Please can I place a spot trade for £327,477.44 to be traded into AUD at the
prevailing rate.

We will need an extended settlement date of the 11th of April please.”

The instruction to place this trade had initially been sent to Curtis Banks on 21 March 2025
by Mr E’s adviser. But the adviser confirmed that:

“The rate has trended upwards since the initial request, so the client should be in a
better position.”

8 April 2025 – Provider T confirmed to Curtis Banks – in relation to a number of outstanding
withdrawals that were still ongoing – that it would accept Curtis Banks’ paperwork. Provider
T apologised for the delay and explained that after internal review and taking into account
the explanation that had been provided, it could now accept the relevant documentation.

Curtis Banks posted the required documents to Provider T; it also sent these to the adviser
so that they could be uploaded to the portal, which they were – all on the same day.

10 April 2025 – Curtis Banks wrote to the adviser confirming that Provider T had confirmed
that the funds had been released that day and that Provider T had applied the information
supplied across all accounts so similar issues shouldn’t be faced going forward.

11 April 2025 – the funds were received by Curtis Banks.

16 April 2025 – Curtis Banks asked Business H for bank account details to enable it to make
payment to settle the trade and this information was provided on the same day.

On the same day, Curtis Banks also confirmed to the adviser that the payment to Business
H had been settled from the SIPP account that day.

2 May 2025 – after some back and forth due to Business H still not being in receipt of the
monies, Curtis Banks confirmed that this was because of an ongoing issue whereby
Business H was rejecting or returning its payments and that it had re-raised the payment that
morning.

On the same day, the adviser relayed an email from Business H confirming that because the
delay was not the fault of the adviser or Curtis Banks, it would honour the rate from the
previously agreed extended settlement date (I note when the transaction completed the
value date for the purchase of Australian dollars was listed as 11 April 2025 – the rate
recorded is 2.05 and £327,477.44 was used to purchase 672,049.20 Australian dollars).

13 May 2025 – Curtis Banks wrote to the adviser confirming that it was in the process of
reconciling the funds that had bounced back from Business H, to enable it to make
payments once Business H could accept payments (following the resolution of the
compliance issues Business H was facing). And, that it had been told that the trades would
not be impacted by the problem, but it did acknowledge that delays to the implementation of
the client strategy would be frustrating in any event.

Separately, Curtis Banks confirmed that Mr E’s payment had been returned to it and that
payment had been made to Business H again that day.

15 May 2025 – Curtis Banks confirmed (to the adviser) that it had been told that the payment
made on 13 May 2025 had been received by Business H.

Background to the complaint

Mr E complained to Curtis Banks about the delays. Curtis Banks issued its final response
letter explaining that it didn’t consider that it was responsible for the delays, but it
acknowledged that its communication should have been better and offered Mr E £100
compensation for this.

Unhappy with its response Mr E referred his complaint to our service.

One of our investigators reviewed the complaint and concluded that it shouldn’t be upheld.
Mr E disagreed and made further submissions.

The investigator reviewed the submissions made and requested additional information.
However, having reviewed this, the investigator’s view remained unchanged, and they
explained this to Mr E, he didn’t accept the outcome reached and asked for the complaint to
be escalated but didn’t make any further submissions.

Because agreement couldn’t be reached, this complaint was passed to me for review. I sent
Curtis Banks and Mr E copies of my provisional decision, explaining that I thought Mr E’s
complaint should be upheld in part but that Curtis Bank’s existing offer to pay £100
compensation was fair and reasonable under the circumstances. Curtis Banks accepted my
provisional decision. Mr E confirmed that he was disappointed in the outcome but didn’t
make any further submissions.
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and reasonable
in the circumstances of this complaint.
The parties to this complaint have provided detailed submissions to support their respective
positions. I’m grateful to them for taking the time to do so. I’ve considered these submissions
in their entirety. However, I trust that they will not take the fact that my decision focuses on
what I consider to be the central issues as a discourtesy. The purpose of this decision is not
to address every point raised in detail, but to set out my findings, on what I consider to be
the main points, and reasons for reaching them.

It’s my role to fairly and reasonably decide if the respondent business (in this case Curtis
Banks) has done anything wrong in respect of the individual circumstances of the complaint
made and – if I find that the business has done something wrong – award appropriate
redress for any material loss or distress and inconvenience suffered by the complainant as a
result of this.

When considering what is fair and reasonable in the circumstances, I need to take account
of relevant law and regulations, regulator’s rules, guidance and standards, codes of practice
and, where appropriate, what I consider to have been good industry practice at the relevant
time. Ultimately, I’m required to make a decision that I consider to be fair and reasonable in
all the circumstances of the case.

Having reviewed Mr E’s complaint, my findings remain as set out in my provisional decision,
I’ve largely reiterated these below.

It’s not in dispute that the transaction about which Mr E complains here took significantly
longer than it ought reasonably to have done – and it is, of course, understandable that this
caused Mr E frustration and worry in addition to any financial impact. However, what I’m
looking at here is whether any material delay was caused by a failing on Curtis Banks’ part.
Having done so, I’m not persuaded that it was, but I do think that its communication – or lack
thereof – at times added to the distress and inconvenience caused by the situation. That
said, I think that Curtis Banks’ offer of £100 compensation for this is fair and reasonable
under the circumstances.

The delay in the withdrawal of monies held with Provider T

In its email of 11 March 2025, Provider T expressly asked for:

“The sig list refers to a PoA document dated 13/08/24 and a board resolution dated
30/01/24, please can we have a copy of these.”

These are the documents that Curtis Banks sent. Provider T was provided with copies of
these on 11 March 2025, 12 March 2025 and 20 March 2025 – albeit I appreciate that
Provider T couldn’t accept the documents by email, but it did have sight of them. And it
wasn’t until 31 March 2025 that Curtis Banks was informed that these were not the
documents that Provider T required to proceed with the withdrawal in this instance.

We have been provided with some conflicting information as to whether the certified
documents were sent by post around 11-12 March 2025. Or if these weren't sent until 20
March 2025. Following on from Provider T highlighting that only one of the documents
attached to an email (11 March 2025) was certified and that it required all of the documents
to be certified, it does appear that Curtis Banks promptly arranged for all of the documents to
be certified. We’ve been provided with copies of the relevant documents with certifications
dated 11 March 2025. And, we’ve been provided with a copy of an email dated 12 March
2025 from Curtis Banks to Provider T resending the requested documents. Elsewhere,
Curtis Banks indicated that these documents weren’t resent until 20 March 2025 because it
wasn’t clear that Provider T would accept these.

In either event, I don’t think that this made a material difference to the timeline of events
here. I say this because it wasn’t until 8 April 2025 that Provider T agreed to accept a
version of a document it required, and in a specific format, from Curtis Banks – and those
negotiations had been ongoing for some time.

Taking everything into account, I don’t think that Curtis Banks acted unreasonably in relation
to this aspect of the transaction or that its actions caused the delay. Curtis Banks appears to
have provided the documents that Provider T requested in good faith. And, ultimately, there
were ongoing discussions between Curtis Banks and Provider T in relation to a document –
a document that was required in relation to Mr E’s withdrawal – which weren’t resolved until
8 April 2025.

Delay in the received monies being sent to Business H

The trade with Business H is dated 1 April 2025 and the value for the currency purchase is
recorded as being as of 11 April 2025. The adviser indicated at the time that the rates had
improved between the point of the initial instruction (21 March 2025) and the date the trade
was placed (1 April 2025). And, Business H agreed to backdate/hold the settlement date as
at 11 April 2025 in recognition of the fact that the delays at that point weren’t caused by
Curtis Banks or the other parties involved.

So, I don’t think that Mr E was disadvantaged by any delays that Curtis Banks caused. I
appreciate that Mr E says he has missed out on interest, but I don’t think that Curtis Banks
acted unreasonably in attempting to make payment using the details provided to it by
Business H and it appears the delays in the funds being received weren’t caused by Curtis
Banks or any issues within its control.

I understand that this has come as a disappointment to Mr E. However, having reconsidered
Mr E’s complaint, I don’t think that these parts of his complaint should be upheld. This is not
a reflection of the seriousness of the issues Mr E complains about – but, rather, that I’m not
persuaded that what’s gone wrong here is because of a failing on Curtis Banks’ part.

Communications in relation to the ongoing issues with the transactions

Although not the focus of Mr E’s complaint, Curtis Banks found that its communication fell
short at times and offered Mr E £100 compensation for any distress and inconvenience this
caused. As I understand it, this offer hasn’t been accepted and the £100 hasn’t been paid.

Having reviewed the timeline of events and the correspondence exchanged throughout, I
agree that at times Curtis Banks failed to proactively provide updates on the process and
what was holding it up and at times failed to respond to update requests promptly. I think
that Curtis Banks’ offer of £100 compensation is fair and reasonable under the
circumstances.
My final decision
My final decision is that I uphold Mr E’s complaint in part. I don’t think that Curtis Banks
Limited caused the delays about which Mr E complains here. I agree that its communication
should have been better, and I think that the £100 offered is fair and reasonable
compensation for this.

Curtis Banks Limited should pay Mr E £100 compensation, if it hasn’t done so already.

Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr E to accept or
reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

Nicola Curnow
Ombudsman

title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6124805 — Nationwide Building Society
text:
DRN-6124805

The complaint

Mr W complains that Nationwide Building Society didn’t do enough to help him when he told
it about a dispute he had over services, paid for in part using his Nationwide debit card.
What happened
In June 2025 Mr W paid for an all-inclusive holiday. He made a partial payment towards the
holiday of £4,653.95 using his Nationwide debit card.
Upon arriving on holiday Mr W found there was a child in the accommodation next door to
him. He believed that accommodation of this type was adult only and so was disappointed to
see this hadn’t been adhered to.
Mr W completed his holiday and when he returned to the UK he asked Nationwide to help
recover a proportion of the money paid. This was because he didn’t think the service
provided was as described.
Nationwide considered his dispute and initially declined to raise a chargeback. It said that
Mr W had stayed in the accommodation for the full duration of the holiday. Nationwide also
said it couldn’t see that the hotel booked was an adult only hotel, suggesting there wasn’t
evidence that the service provided wasn’t as described.
Unhappy with Nationwide’s response, Mr W referred his complaint to our service. I
understand that after this time Nationwide agreed to raise a chargeback as a gesture of
goodwill.
One of our investigators considered the complaint and didn’t uphold it. They thought it was
fair that Nationwide initially decided not to raise the chargeback. They explained that under
the scheme rules, a chargeback for services not provided can only be made on the unused
portion of the service. However, Mr W used the accommodation for the duration of his
booking and so there was no unused portion to recover.
Mr W had also made arguments in relation to s.75 of the Consumer Credit Act 1974 (CCA).
However, the investigator explained that s.75 CCA doesn’t apply to debit card transactions.
So, Mr W couldn’t make a s.75 CCA claim with respect to his debit card transaction.
In response, Mr W didn’t agree. He argued:
•
That using the service provided was irrelevant to the card scheme rules, DISP or the
Consumer Rights Act 2015 (CRA) as the correct test is, was the service provided as
described.
•
The card scheme rules do not state that accessing or using a service prevents a
chargeback.
•
The merchant sold an adult-only room type which wasn’t provided. Under the CRA
services must match their description and be delivered with reasonable care. This
was not delivered.

•
Nationwide failed to consider the complaint in line with DISP and the investigator
didn’t apply the correct test when considering the complaint.
•
Nationwide failed to consider if another dispute code would have been more
appropriate.
As an agreement hasn’t been reached, the complaint has been passed to me to consider.
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Having done so, I’m not going to uphold this complaint. I appreciate this will be disappointing
to Mr W. But I think Nationwide handled his chargeback dispute fairly.
I’ve read everything that the parties have said, but I’ll concentrate my comments on what I
think is relevant. If I don’t comment on a specific point it’s not because I’ve failed to consider
it, but because I don’t think I need to comment in order to reach a fair and reasonable
outcome. And our rules allow me to do this. This reflects the nature of our service as a free
and informal alternative to the courts.

Chargeback

A chargeback is the process by which payment settlement disputes are resolved between
card issuers and merchants, under the relevant card scheme rules. It allows customers to
ask for a transaction to be refunded in a number of situations, some common examples
being where goods or services aren’t provided, or where goods or services aren’t as
described.

There's no automatic right to a chargeback; the chargeback process doesn’t give consumers
legal rights; and chargeback is not a guaranteed method of getting a refund because
chargebacks may be defended by the merchant. This is because the rules, set out by the
card scheme lay down strict conditions which must be satisfied for a chargeback claim to
succeed. If a financial business thinks that a claim won't be successful, it doesn’t have to
raise a chargeback. But where there’s a reasonable chance of success, I’d expect a financial
business to raise a chargeback.

In this case Mr W raised a dispute with Nationwide. He argued that the service provided
wasn’t as described because he booked adult-only accommodation which wasn’t provided.
The relevant card scheme operator in this case was VISA, and Nationwide considered
whether it could raise a chargeback on Mr W’s behalf under the reason code goods or
services “not as described or defective merchandise/services.” I think that based on what
Mr W has said, this was the most applicable reason code. So, it was reasonable that Mr W’s
chargeback was considered under this reason code.

The VISA scheme rules which were applicable at the time clearly state that the disputed
payment is only limited to the “unused portion of the cancelled service.” It’s not in dispute
that Mr W used the accommodation for the full period he booked. So, I don’t think he
would’ve been able to chargeback any amount as there was no unused portion of his
holiday. I therefore think it was fair for Nationwide to initially decide Mr W’s chargeback had
no prospect for success and not to raise it.

I note Mr W has argued that whether there was an unused portion of accommodation
remaining isn’t the correct test and Nationwide should have considered if the service was as

described. I can appreciate why Mr W has argued this but unfortunately, I don’t agree.
Even if the service wasn’t provided as described, and for the avoidance of doubt I don’t
agree that was the case, any funds recovered via chargeback in these circumstances are
limited to the unused portion. So, the fact Mr W used the accommodation in full is relevant to
considering whether he had a reasonable prospect of recovering the funds paid under this
chargeback reason code. And given he used the accommodation in full, I don’t think his
chargeback claim had any reasonable prospect for success. So, I think Nationwide’s initial
decision not to raise the chargeback was fair and reasonable in the circumstances.

I also think it’s important to highlight that even though his chargeback had no real prospect
for success, Nationwide still explained why it also didn’t agree the service wasn’t as
described. And when Mr W continued to dispute the payment Nationwide subsequently
submitted a chargeback as a gesture of goodwill. So, I think Nationwide has gone further
than I would have expected it to.

Mr W has raised the protections afforded to him by the CRA and argued Nationwide should
have considered this. However, as I’ve explained above, a chargeback is a voluntary
scheme, which is decided by the scheme operator (in this case VISA). It doesn’t convey
legal rights and is subject to the scheme rules. As such Nationwide isn’t required to consider
the Mr W’s rights under the CRA as part of a chargeback.

Finally, I’ve noted that Mr W has argued Nationwide’s response to the dispute fails to comply
with the Financial Conduct Authority’s Handbook, Dispute Handling Rules (“DISP”). As it
didn’t investigate properly or apply the correct test. I disagree Nationwide’s investigation
breached DISP. Nationwide considered the information provided and concluded in the first
instance that Mr W’s chargeback had a limited prospect for success. It also relied on the
VISA chargeback rules to reach this conclusion, as it was required to do.

My final decision
My final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint against Nationwide Building Society.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr W to accept or
reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

Claire Lisle
Ombudsman

title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6339594 — esure Insurance Limited
text:
DRN-6339594

The complaint

Mr C has complained about how esure Insurance Limited trading as Sheilas' Wheels (esure)
handled a claim he made on his motor insurance policy.
Where I refer to esure below, this includes the actions of their agents.
What happened
Mr C was involved in a motor accident in December 2024 and made a claim on his motor
insurance policy with esure. esure accepted the claim and sought to treat it as a total loss.
Mr C wasn’t happy about the amount esure would deduct for salvage. He ultimately withdrew
the claim and settled with the third-party insurer directly. And esure marked the claim as
‘notification only’ on relevant databases.
Mr C made several complaints to esure about how they handled things throughout the life of
the claim. esure issued complaint responses in January and February 2025 not upholding Mr
C’s complaints. They maintained their stance on dealing with the claim on a total loss basis
and on how much they would pay for the salvage.
Mr C referred his complaint to this Service. When this Service asked esure for information,
they reconsidered what happened and acknowledged service failings – and they offered
£200 compensation to try to put things right. An Investigator looked into what happened and
felt esure didn’t handle things the way they should have, but that esure’s offer of
compensation was fair. Mr C didn’t think this resolved things, and the complaint was passed
to me to decide.
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and reasonable
in the circumstances of this complaint.
As ours is an informal service, I’m not going to comment on every point or piece of evidence
Mr C and esure sent us. Instead, I’ve focused on what I consider to be key or central to the
complaint. But I’d like to reassure both parties that I have considered everything submitted.

I’ve considered whether esure handled the claim promptly and fairly between the date of the
accident and their February 2025 complaint response letter. Mr C told this Service that the
claim was dealt directly with the third-party insurer, and I note he hasn’t suffered any
financial loss – so I don’t need to comment on whether esure caused any. So, I’ve focused
my findings below on whether the salvage amount esure intended to deduct was reasonable,
and whether esure communicated with Mr C in a way that was fair, clear, and not
misleading.
Mr C’s policy says that after his vehicle is involved in an accident esure will:
• Decide to pay to get it fixed, or
• Replace what’s been lost or damaged, or

• Pay for what’s been lost or damaged
And that esure will decide which of these methods will be used to settle his claim. So, it’s
esure’s choice whether to pay him an amount to replace his vehicle. In this case, esure
considered the cost of repairing the vehicle would be beyond economical repair, so they
opted to write off the vehicle and pay Mr C its market value. There’s no dispute between
esure and Mr C about the valuation of the vehicle, so I don’t need to comment on this. And,
given the estimated repair cost was was around 72% of the market value, I don’t find esure’s
intention to treat the vehicle as a total loss unreasonable.
Mr C’s policy says after making the payment for a total loss, the vehicle will belong to esure.
But it’s not unusual for an insurer to allow a policyholder to retain the salvage of their vehicle.
And when that happens, it’s also not unusual for that insurer to deduct what they would have
received when disposing of the salvage itself. This is because, when an insurer pays out for
a total loss, they’ll usually get to retain the damaged vehicle if it’s available.
Since esure were intending to write off the vehicle because they considered it beyond
economical repair, they would have been entitled to retain it in exchange for paying Mr C a
fair market value. Or, if Mr C opted to keep the vehicle, they could deduct an amount they
would have received for the salvage.
Mr C said the amount of deduction for the salvage wasn’t reasonable as he received quotes
that were much lower. Insurers often have arrangements with salvage agents which are
more favourable than what is available to private individuals, and I’m satisfied what esure
said they could get was reasonable.
Having looked over the claim communications more generally, I find that esure acted unfairly
in their handling of the claim at times, and that this has caused some distress and
inconvenience to Mr C for which compensation is warranted. This included instances where
esure gave conflicting information to Mr C about sharing third-party insurer details; about
whether they would need to inspect the vehicle or if Mr C could use his own repairer; and
about whether they intended to treat the vehicle as a total loss or carry out repairs. I’m
satisfied the £200 compensation esure have offered is appropriate in the circumstances, and
I’m directing them to pay this amount.
My final decision
I uphold this complaint and direct esure Insurance Limited trading as Sheilas' Wheels to pay
Mr C the £200 they offered.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr C to accept or
reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

Andrew Wakatsuki-Robinson
Ombudsman

title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6347526 — Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited
text:
DRN-6347526

The complaint

Mr K complains that Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited (‘Aviva’) repeatedly sent him
correspondence by post despite his instructions not to do so as he wasn’t resident at the
address at the time. He says that these repeated errors have caused him a significant
amount of concern, distress and inconvenience.

What happened
We’ve been provided with information by Mr K and Aviva, including copies of the
correspondence exchanged. The below is an overview of the events that led to Mr K raising
this complaint, it isn’t an account of all of the correspondence exchanged or submissions
made. For the avoidance of doubt, I’ve read and considered all of the information provided
by both parties.

Mr K has a pension with Aviva and – due to him not residing at his registered address – has
requested no post is issued to him and all correspondence be sent by email. Despite this
request being on his file, correspondence was repeatedly issued by post for various reasons,
to addresses where tenants were residing. Mr K complained about this on a number of
occasions.

Most recently, Mr K called Aviva to arrange a withdrawal and at the same time updated his
“care of” address. He reiterated during his call that he wanted to receive everything by email
and that he still wasn’t a UK resident – but, following this, correspondence was issued to the
updated address.

Background to the complaint

Unhappy that his instructions hadn’t been followed and concerned that his personal
information had once again been sent to an address where other people were – and he
wasn’t – residing, Mr K raised a complaint. Aviva upheld Mr K’s complaint and ultimately
paid him a total of £200 compensation (initially £150 then a further £50). Unhappy with its
responses, Mr K referred his complaint to this service.

One of our investigators reviewed the complaint and concluded that:

•
The correspondence sent in error that was the subject of previous complaints
couldn’t now be considered by our service, because the complaints hadn’t been
referred to us within six months of the respective final response letters issued.
•
We could consider Mr K’s complaint about correspondence recently issued in error to
his UK address – but, that the compensation Aviva had paid in respect of this was
fair and reasonable under the circumstances.

Mr K disagreed with the outcome reached. He said that due to the nature of the problem he
only became aware that the problem hadn’t been resolved when subsequent
correspondence was issued, which wouldn’t necessarily happen within the six months. So,
strict application of the six-month time limit risks the ongoing errors not being properly
considered despite them relating to the same underlying issue. He relied on Aviva’s

repeated assurances that the issue had been resolved. Living abroad Mr K says that he had
limited ability to monitor and manage the situation and this – along with the
ongoing/recurring nature of the problem – contributed to the level of concern and distress he
experienced.

Because agreement couldn’t be reached, this case was passed to me for review.

What I’ve decided – and why – jurisdiction

We can’t consider all complaints referred to this service. Before we can consider something,
we need to check, by reference to the Financial Conduct Authority’s (‘FCA’) DISP Rules and
the legislation from which those rules are derived, whether the complaint is one we have the
power to look at and whether it’s a complaint we should consider.

I’ve carefully considered these rules when deciding Mr K’s complaint along with all the
submissions made throughout the course of this complaint. Having done so, like the
investigator, I’ve found that aspects (detailed below) of Mr K’s complaint aren’t ones that we
can consider.

Within this section of the decision, I haven’t set out the details of what happened and the
nature of Mr K’s complaint and submissions in the same detail that I might ordinarily, if I
were considering the merits of these parts of Mr K’s complaint. That is because this part of
my decision is solely in relation to our jurisdiction to consider Mr K’s complaint or parts of his
complaint.

The six-month rule

DISP 2.8.2R sets out that:

“The Ombudsman cannot consider a complaint if the complainant refers it to the
Financial Ombudsman Service:

(1) more than six months after the date on which the respondent sent the
complainant its final response, redress determination or summary resolution
communication;

…

unless:

(3) in the view of the Ombudsman, the failure to comply with the time limits in DISP
2.8.2 R or DISP 2.8.7 R was as a result of exceptional circumstances; …

(5) the respondent has consented to the Ombudsman considering the complaint
where the time limits in DISP 2.8.2 R or DISP 2.8.7 R have expired”

This means that, we can’t consider a complaint where it’s been made:

•
More than six months after the date on which the respondent sent the complainant its
final response; unless
•
The business consents to us looking into the complaint despite it having been made
late; or
•
Exceptional circumstances apply, for example, where the complainant has been
incapacitated – and, as a result of this, was unable to bring the complaint to this
service within the applicable time limits.

The issues that Mr K has faced with correspondence being sent to his UK addresses have
been ongoing for some time. Mr K has complained about this on multiple occasions, and, in
turn, Aviva has issued a number of final response letters (for example, those dated: 5
January 2022, 11 February 2022 and 25 October 2023).

As set out above – and as explained by the investigator – where a final response letter is
issued the complainant (in this case Mr K) has six months to refer the complaint to us. If the
complaint isn’t referred to us within six months – barring any exceptional circumstances – we
can’t then consider the merits of that complaint, unless the business consents to us doing
so, which in this case Aviva hasn’t.

Mr K has explained that – due to the nature of the complaint – he reasonably considered the
issue to be resolved at each juncture until the next time correspondence was issued in error
to his UK addresses. And that due to the regularity with which this happened, he wasn’t in a
position to escalate the complaints within six months of the respective final response letters.

I can appreciate Mr K’s position in relation to this however I’m not persuaded that this alters
the application of the six-month time limit, and I don’t think that this prevented him from
referring a complaint to this service about the existing issues addressed by any of the final
response letters within six months of those respective letters. So, I’m not persuaded that
exceptional circumstances apply here.

Taking everything into account, like the investigator, I’ve found that we can’t consider the
merits of Mr K’s prior complaints relating broadly to the same ongoing issue. Mr K’s most
recent complaint was referred to us in time, and I’ve set out my findings on that complaint
below.

What I’ve decided – and why – merits of the complaint
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
It’s my role to fairly and reasonably decide if the respondent business (in this case Aviva)
has done anything wrong in respect of the individual circumstances of the complaint made
and – if I find that the business has done something wrong – award appropriate redress for
any material loss or distress and inconvenience suffered by the complainant as a result of
this.

When considering what is fair and reasonable in the circumstances, I need to take account
of relevant law and regulations, regulator’s rules, guidance and standards, codes of practice
and, where appropriate, what I consider to have been good industry practice at the relevant
time. Ultimately, I’m required to make a decision that I consider to be fair and reasonable in
all the circumstances of the case.

The parties to this complaint have provided detailed submissions to support their respective
positions. I’m grateful to them for taking the time to do so. I’ve considered these submissions
in their entirety. However, I trust that they will not take the fact that my decision focuses on
what I consider to be the central issues as a discourtesy. The purpose of this decision is not
to address every point raised in detail, but to set out my findings, on what I consider to be
the main points, and reasons for reaching them.

As I’ve mentioned above, the failings Mr K previously complained (in earlier complaints) to
Aviva about can’t now be considered by this Service. However, I think the fact that Mr K
faced ongoing issues and administrative errors is relevant to considering the impact the

issues we can consider had on him and the concern that these caused. And I’ve taken this
into consideration in determining whether the amount of compensation Aviva paid Mr K is
fair and reasonable under the circumstances.

Aviva has paid Mr K a total of £200 in respect of issues he’s complained about that were
referred to us within the time limits, it has also updated his address to an internal business
address, with a view to preventing any automated correspondence issued from being sent to
Mr K’s UK addresses.

Having personal financial information sent to an address where someone else is residing (as
I understand it tenants renting the property) will understandably have caused Mr K distress
and worry. And, I think this will have been made worse by this being something that had
happened multiple times before and that Mr K considered had been done in error and on
each occasion had been resolved.

I’ve carefully considered everything that Mr K has told us about the impact that this has had
on him. Having done so, I think that the amount of compensation that Aviva has paid is fair
and reasonable and in line with the type of award that we would have made had it not
already paid compensation.

I understand that this decision will likely come as a significant disappointment to Mr K, it is
clear from his complaint submissions that he feels strongly about the issues he has raised.
My final decision
For the reasons set out above, I find that we can’t consider the events that were the subject
of prior complaints. We can consider the merits of Mr K’s current complaint, but my final
decision is that I don’t uphold Mr K’s complaint about Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited and I
make no award.

Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr K to accept or
reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

Nicola Curnow
Ombudsman

title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6397524 — Wise Payments Limited
text:
DRN-6397524

The complaint

S is a company, and this complaint has been brought on its behalf by its director, whom I’ll
refer to as “R”. S complains that Wise Payments Limited failed to provide it with appropriate
assistance after it blocked the company’s account.
What happened
In March 2026 Wise carried out a review of S’s account. As a result of that review, it asked
S, through R, to provide proof of its trading address. Wise placed restrictions on the account
pending provision of that proof. Until that point, it appears that the address which S used
was the address of its registered office, rather than one which it used to conduct its
business.
Wise explained that a trading address needed to be one from which a company’s business
operations were carried out, such as a home office or shop premises. Failing that, it could be
the home address of the director. R has explained that he works remotely, so it is difficult for
him and S to meet those criteria.
On or about 28 March 2026 R provided a copy of a bank statement, addressed to him, which
he said met Wise’s requirements. Wise did not agree and said it would not lift the restrictions
on the account. The address on the statement was not the same as S’s registered address.
On 23 April 2026 R updated the address again and submitted further documents to Wise
which he said this met its requirements of a trading address. This time, Wise accepted the
documents, and the account restrictions were lifted on 25 April 2026.
R does not dispute that Wise was entitled to seek proof of S’s trading address or that it could
restrict the account in the meantime. But he says that, while the account was restricted,
Wise failed to support S or to take active steps to identify or suggest a solution to the
difficulty of not having a trading address.
Wise paid S £120 in recognition of the inconvenience it had suffered as a result of delays. R
did not accept that and referred the matter to this service. One of our investigators
considered what had happened but took the view that the compensation already paid was
enough to resolve matters. R asked that an ombudsman review the case.
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
I have reviewed the copies of the webchats between R and Wise over the period of around a
month when the account was restricted. I have some sympathy with him. On a number of
occasions, he was told that the matter had been escalated, but there is no real indication
that this made any difference. R was also told on several occasions that he needed to
provide documents which he had either already provided but which had been rejected, or
which he had said he could not provide. Wise has acknowledged that there was a “… delay

in communication and an expectation gap regarding the resolution pathway..”. I take that to
be an admission that Wise did not handle R’s enquiries as well as it should have done.
Nevertheless, I accept that Wise did not have the documents it needed until around 23 April
2026. The documents provided before that did not prove S’s trading address, even given the
broad definition used by Wise.
R has said that S has suffered actual financial loss and damage to its reputation as a result
of Wise’s actions. He has estimated those losses at around £3,500. He has not, however,
provided any evidence to support that assertion, and I do not therefore believe it would be
fair to make an award in respect of those alleged losses.
Wise did agree however to pay £120 to recognise the inconvenience suffered, and I agree
with the investigator that that is reasonable in all the circumstances. I do not believe it would
be fair or reasonable to award any more.
My final decision
For these reasons, my final decision is that I do not uphold S’s complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask S to accept or
reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

Mike Ingram
Ombudsman

title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6400588 — HSBC UK Bank Plc
text:
DRN-6400588

The complaint

Mrs and Mr K complain that after HSBC UK Bank Plc deactivated and reactivated their
access to online and mobile banking they were unable to view and manage future payments.

What happened
Mrs and Mr K hold a joint account with HSBC in the UK. They also hold an HSBC account
overseas.

For many years Mrs and Mr K made a regular monthly payment from their UK HSBC
account to an HSBC account they hold overseas. They said they’d been able to view and
manage this payment via the “future payments” online and mobile banking facility. However,
because of errors by Mrs and Mr K with security telephone verification, their account was
frozen. This resulted in their access to online and mobile banking being suspended. After
their account and online and mobile banking abilities were reactivated, the future payments
facility no longer showed the payment Mrs and Mr K had made to their overseas account
each month. However, the payments continued to be made each month as a recurring
payment.

Mrs and Mr K contacted HSBC and asked it to explain why they were unable to see their
payments in the future payments section of their online banking and app. They said they
spent significant periods of time speaking with HSBC by telephone and online webchat
about this issue. They said this process was protracted and HSBC and that it didn’t provide
an explanation about what had happened or how to remedy the issue. They thought the
service they’d received from HSBC when discussing the problem was poor and confusing.
So, they complained.

HSBC investigated Mrs and Mr K’s concerns and issued its final response to their complaint
on 18 November 2025. Within that correspondence, HSBC apologised for what had
happened. It informed Mrs and Mr K the problem they were complaining about was a known
issue that would occur where an account had been frozen and access to online and mobile
banking had been suspended. It explained the steps they’d need to take in order to set up
the payment in the way they wanted. HSBC didn’t think a banking error had caused the
issue with Mrs and Mr K’s payment. But it acknowledged that communication could have
been clearer. It paid Mrs and Mr K £100 in compensation to resolve this part of their
complaint. However, it subsequently debited and then re-credited his sum.

Being dissatisfied with HSBC’s response to their complaint, Mrs and Mr K referred it to our
service. Our investigator empathised with them but didn’t recommend upholding their
complaint. They were persuaded, overall, that HSBC had offered helpful guidance to Mrs
and Mr K in how to set up their regular payment in the way they wanted. And they thought its
payment of £100 was fair and reasonable for the shortfalls in communication. So, they didn’t
recommend it take further action to resolve the complaint.

HSBC accepted our investigator’s view on the merits of this complaint. But Mrs and Mr K
disagreed and asked an ombudsman to decide their complaint. I’ve therefore been asked to
decide the fairest way of resolving matters.

What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
I’m sorry to hear about the difficulties Mrs and Mr K experienced here. I know they feel very
strongly about this matter and I appreciate the reasons they brought their complaint to our
service. However, while I sympathise with them, the issue that I must determine is whether
HSBC made a mistake, or treated Mrs and Mr K unfairly, such that it needs to now put things
right.

This service is an informal dispute resolution service. When considering what’s fair and
reasonable, I’m required to take into account a number of matters, which include relevant
law and regulations, regulators’ rules, guidance and standards, codes of practice, the terms
and conditions of any insurance policy and, where appropriate, what I consider to have been
good industry practice at the relevant time. I’m not limited to the position a court might reach.

Within this final decision I’ll concentrate my findings on what I think is relevant to decide this
complaint, which is reflective of our approach in assessing complaints. This means that I
may not comment on every written representation made by Mrs and Mr K and HSBC, which
is because I don’t think I need to comment on it to reach what I think is the right outcome.

Based on the records HSBC has provided, I’m satisfied that the problems with the monthly
payment, which led to this complaint, were caused by Mrs and Mr K’s account being frozen
and access to their online and mobile banking being suspended. This step was taken by
HSBC due to Mrs and Mr K failing security verification procedures. Our service views this as
reasonable action to protect a customer’s account from potential fraud and unauthorised
access.

HSBC has stated after Mrs and Mr K’s access to their account and online and mobile
banking was reinstated, their monthly payment wasn’t showing as a future payment. While
I’ve no doubt this was frustrating, this is a known issue that occurs where an account had
been frozen and access to online and mobile banking has been suspended. I understand
that Mrs and Mr K didn’t suffer financially as a result of this issue because the payment
continued to be made even though it wasn’t showing within the future payment facility of
their online banking.

I’ve carefully considered what HSBC did to assist Mrs and Mr K in resolving their concerns
about their payment. The evidence provided by HSBC satisfies me that communication
between it and Mrs and Mr K was protracted. There was a lot of back and forth between both
parties. It’s clear from the written correspondence HSBC has shared with our service that
communication with Mrs and Mr K broke down at times, which caused frustration and upset.

Set against the poor communication I’ve outlined above, I can see that HSBC provided clear
guidance and instruction to Mrs and Mr K about how to set up and manage their payment in
the way they wanted. It explained that to resolve the issue, they’d need to cancel the regular
payment and set it up again. It told them that taking this action would make the new transfer
visible under the “Manage Future Payments” section in their online and mobile banking
facility. I haven’t identified any further assistance that HSBC could have meaningfully
provided here.

I’m pleased to see that HSBC acknowledged the shortfalls in communication and apologised
for this. It paid Mrs and Mr K compensation of £100 for what happened. So, I’ve considered
whether this is fair and reasonable.

Our service isn’t here to punish businesses. When deciding what potential compensation to
award our service must take two things into account: financial loss because of any business
error and non-financial loss, including inconvenience and upset.

In relation to financial loss, I’ve haven’t seen any evidence that demonstrates that Mrs and
Mr K incurred a financial loss as a result of shortfalls in communication. It follows that I’m not
making an award for financial loss.

Turning now to awards for non-financial loss there isn’t a set formula that we use to calculate
awards for particular errors. It’s my role to consider what impact HSBC’s actions had on Mrs
and Mr K and to decide, within guidelines set by our service, what an appropriate amount of
compensation might be.

I recognise that the shortfalls in communication would have caused some frustration and
inconvenience to Mrs and Mr K. However, having had regard to our guidelines, I’m
persuaded that £100 is a fair and reasonable amount of compensation that reflects the
trouble and upset they’d have experienced here. It’s consistent with awards our service has
made in comparable circumstances and it’s what I’d have suggested had no offer been
made. So, I won’t be requiring HSBC to increase that amount to resolve this complaint.

I’m aware that HSBC paid £100 directly into Mrs and Mr K’s account. While it debited this
amount shortly afterwards, it re-credited the funds once it realised this payment had been
reversed. I recognise that this was frustrating and upsetting for Mrs and Mr K. However, like
our investigator, I’m satisfied that this was a genuine error on HSBC’s part. It’s apologised
for its mistake and, by re-crediting Mrs and Mr K’s account with £100, I’m satisfied it’s put
them back in the position they’d have been in had the error not occurred. While Mrs and Mr
K may disagree with me, I’m satisfied an apology is sufficient to resolve this part of their
complaint. So, I’m not going to direct HSBC to do anything further.

I understand that Mrs and Mr K feel very strongly about the issues raised in this complaint
and I’ve carefully considered everything they’ve said. But, based on the evidence I’ve seen, I
think HSBC has acted fairly and reasonably in how it dealt with this complaint. This now
brings to an end what we, in trying to resolve Mrs and Mr K’s dispute with HSBC, can do for
them. I’m sorry we can’t help Mrs and Mr K any further with this complaint.

My final decision
My final decision is that I don’t uphold this complaint.

Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mrs K and Mr K to
accept or reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

Julie Mitchell
Ombudsman

title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6318545 — Everyday Lending Limited
text:
DRN-6318545

The complaint

Mr G complains that Everyday Lending Limited, trading as Evlo, mis-sold a loan to him in
January 2025.
The loan was for £7,500, repayable over four years with monthly repayments of around
£335, with an APR of 55.4%.
What happened
Mr G applied for a loan in December 2024, which was approved and disbursed by Evlo in
January 2025.
Mr G says the loan was mis-sold, because he only took the loan out to improve his credit
score and the funds weren’t actually required. He also complains that the cost of the loan
was disproportionate and he felt under pressure to agree to the loan.
Mr G complained to Evlo who didn’t uphold his complaint.
Mr G brought his complaint to our service and an investigator considered its merits, but
thought that Evlo hadn’t done anything wrong.
Mr G didn’t agree and asked for an ombudsman to decide.
What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Having done so, I’m not upholding this complaint. I know this will disappoint Mr G, so I’ll
explain why.
When Mr G applied for the loan, he said it was to pay for a heating system for his mum and
this remained consistent throughout all the discussions he had with Evlo.
There were a number of calls during December 2024 and January 2025, which I have
listened to, many of which relate to Mr G’s income and expenditure.
Below, I refer only to the key points that are pertinent to my decision. Mr G has also been
clear that he isn’t complaining the loan was unaffordable.
It is in one of the first calls between Mr G and Evlo, on 16 December 2024, where he
explains that the loan is to pay for a heating system for his mum.
There is no reference in that call about his credit score, but in subsequent calls Mr G makes
references to wanting to improve his credit score, as he will be looking to take out a
mortgage in around 12 months’ time.
On 10 January 2025, Mr G’s credit score is discussed with Evlo in a call that I’ve listened to.
Within this call there are discussions about Mr G using some of the loan to pay off some
balances on existing credit.
Evlo’s agent explains, in fairly generic terms, how doing so and keeping up with the
payments for the loan, could improve his credit score. But there is nothing Evlo has said in
this call, or any of the others, that could be reasonably construed as advising Mr G to take

the loan simply to improve his credit score, or guarantee that it would do so. I refer to this
again below.
As noted above, the interest rate for this loan was 55.4% APR, and Mr G thinks this is
disproportionately high.
Evlo describes itself as a lender who specialises in providing credit for those with less-than-
perfect credit history. Interest rates will vary across the industry, depending on the specific
circumstances of the individual applying for a loan, and these may well be higher than for a
customer with a good credit history.
The interest rates and repayment terms for the loan that Evlo provided to Mr G were clearly
explained to him, including within the call on 10 January 2025. In it, Mr G and Evlo have a
discussion about the interest rates and Mr G’s future plans. With regards to his credit score,
Mr G explains that he hopes to be able to have better rates available to him in the future,
agreeing with Evlo that in general terms, this could be a stepping stone.
Mr G also signed some documents, also dated 10 January 2025, where he specifically put
his initials to confirm that, among other things, he knew his loan amount, APR and total
repayable. He also signed a loan agreement, where the details of the loan were clearly laid
out.
I acknowledge that Mr G feels that the interest rate is disproportionately high, but I’m
comfortable that all of the specifics about the cost were clearly explained to him, both in
writing and over the phone. So I do consider that Evlo provided him with all the necessary
information for him to be able to make an informed decision on whether to proceed with the
loan.
Having listened to all of the calls between Mr G and Evlo from 16 December 2024 and 10
January 2025, there is nothing to indicate that Mr G was being pressured and nothing to
suggest that he felt that way at the time.
The documents that Mr G signed, which I have referred to above, also include details of the
14 day “cooling off period” where Mr G could return the funds in full and end the agreement.
This was also explained to him in one of the calls on 10 January 2025, in which he also
refers to the service he has received from Evlo as “fantastic”.
In conclusion, I haven’t found that Evlo has done anything wrong in the circumstances of this
complaint, during the loan application, assessment or approval stages, so I don’t uphold this
complaint.
In reaching my conclusions, I’ve also considered whether the relationship between Mr G and
Evlo might have been unfair to Mr G under Section 140A of the Consumer Credit Act 1974
(“CCA”). However, for the reasons I’ve already explained, I’m satisfied that Evlo did not treat
Mr G unfairly in relation to this matter. And I haven’t seen anything to suggest that Section
140A of the CCA would, given the facts of this complaint, lead to a different outcome here.
My final decision
For the reasons outlined above, my final decision is that I’m not upholding this complaint
against Everyday Lending Limited, trading as Evlo.

Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mr G to accept or
reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

David Barker
Ombudsman

title: Ombudsman decision DRN-6158520 — NATIONAL WESTMINSTER BANK PUBLIC LIMITED COMPANY
text:
DRN-6158520

The complaint

Mrs J complains that NATIONAL WESTMINSTER BANK PUBLIC LIMITED COMPANY
(NatWest) has applied interest and charges to her overdraft account.

What happened
Mrs J has an overdraft account with NatWest. The account was being managed by
NatWest’s Specialist Support Team (SST), but she says this support was removed without
her knowledge. And in June 2025, Mrs J says that interest and charges recommenced,
which she feels is unfair given her circumstances.

Mrs J doesn’t feel that NatWest should be charging her interest on the overdraft – she says
that interest started without prior notice and while she was vulnerable with an active
complaint. She says that due to the charges, she has been forced to borrow money from
family.

NatWest responded to Mrs J’s complaint; and it explained that the SST had tried to get in
touch with her, but because it didn’t receive a reply, her account was passed back to its
collections team and then later interest resumed. It said that interest and charges had been
applied in line with the terms and conditions of the account since June 2025, and it didn’t
think it had done anything wrong. Despite NatWest saying that it hadn’t done anything wrong
in relation to Mrs J’s overdraft account, it refunded £100 to her. And it explained that if Mrs J
still required support from SST; then she could contact it and it would review her situation.

An Investigator considered the information provided by both parties, but they didn’t think
NatWest had treated Mrs J unfairly or unreasonably. The Investigator explained that this
service could only consider Mrs J’s complaint about the interest being reapplied from June
2025, as this service had already considered Mrs J’s complaint about previous interest
charges; and so we wouldn’t consider this again. The Investigator explained that NatWest
were entitled to start charging interest, and it hadn’t acted unfairly in doing so.

Mrs J didn’t agree with the Investigator’s view, and I have summarised her main points
below:

•
She didn’t receive the letter SST sent to her in April 2025; and there is no proof the
letter was delivered. NatWest made no attempt to contact her in any other way.
•
She explained that she is on benefits, a single parent, signed off with mental illness
and dealing with PTSD. NatWest knew this and shouldn’t have assumed she could
afford interest to restart without any assessment of her affordability or vulnerability.
•
Her overdraft debt hasn’t ever reduced despite her making repayments.
•
NatWest didn’t help her when she asked for support.
•
Mrs J says that she did contact NatWest during this time period, as she did so to
dispute the charges and raise further complaints.

Because an agreement couldn’t be reached, the complaint has been passed to me to decide
on the matter.

What I’ve decided – and why
I’ve considered all the available evidence and arguments to decide what’s fair and
reasonable in the circumstances of this complaint.
Having considered all of the evidence available, I don’t uphold Mrs J’s complaint. I
appreciate this decision will come as a disappointment to her, as I can see how strongly she
feels about what’s happened in her case, however I will explain how I have reached my
outcome below.

Before I do that, I want to make it clear that I have read and taken into account all of the
information provided by both parties, in reaching my decision. If I’ve not reflected something
that’s been said it’s not because I didn’t see it, it’s because I didn’t deem it relevant to the
crux of the complaint. This isn’t intended as a discourtesy to either party, but merely to
reflect my informal role in deciding what a fair and reasonable outcome is. This also means I
don’t think it’s necessary to get an answer, or provide my own answer, to every question
raised unless I think it’s relevant to the crux of the complaint.

Ultimately, Mrs J’s complaint here is about NatWest having applied interest to her account in
June 2025, and the following months. So I have considered this to be the main crux of the
complaint, and I’ll focus my decision on whether it was fair and reasonable of it to have done
this, in the circumstances of Mrs J’s complaint.

NatWest has said that it wrote to Mrs J in April 2025, to see if she still needed the support of
the SST. It says it asked Mrs J to get in touch with it; and because it didn’t hear from her, her
account was no longer being managed by SST; and because her overdraft was now within
the limit, interest and charges started to accrue again.

Mrs J says she didn’t get the letter NatWest says it sent her in April 2025, so she had no
idea that she needed to contact NatWest or that it intended to remove the support that was
in place for her. She also says she had no idea that NatWest intended to charge interest to
her account.

NatWest said it no longer has a copy of the letter it says it sent to Mrs J in April 2025. I can
see from the notes provided by NatWest that these show a letter was sent, but because I
haven’t seen a copy of the letter, I don’t know where the letter was sent to, or what it said.
And because of this, I’m minded concluding that it is possible Mrs J didn’t get the letter. And
so, she didn’t contact NatWest because she didn’t know she needed to. I can also see from
NatWest’s contact notes added just weeks before it sent her the letter, that it noted she
should be contacted by email only; it isn’t clear to me why it then sent her a letter. So I do
think NatWest could have done more to try and contact Mrs J. That said, I can see that
NatWest has explained that Mrs J can still receive support from the SST if she feels this is
necessary; and she would need to contact NatWest about this. I think this is reasonable in
the circumstances.

Even if Mrs J had received the letter and requested to still be under the control of the SST, I
don’t think this would likely have impacted the ultimate position of her account. I say this
because NatWest has explained that Mrs J’s account was then within its overdraft limit; and
so interest and charges would have resumed in line with the terms and conditions of the
account – there isn’t anything unreasonable about this; and there is no requirement for
NatWest to suspend interest and charges indefinitely. So I don’t think it was unfair or
unreasonable of NatWest to have resumed interest when it did. There also isn’t a

requirement for NatWest to stop interest and charges while a complaint is ongoing – so I’m
also not of the view that it has done anything wrong for this reason either.

Mrs J has said that she wasn’t aware that NatWest were going to start charging her interest
again. NatWest explained that it would have made her aware prior to doing so. I haven’t
seen any evidence to suggest that it did in fact pre-warn her about the re-commencement of
interest; this doesn’t mean it didn’t, I just haven’t seen evidence of such. But again, even if
Mrs J had received notification of this, this wouldn’t have meant interest and charges would
have been stopped. I do accept though that it would have likely been a shock for Mrs J to
have seen that she was being charged interest again – especially if she hadn’t been made
aware before it happened. That said, I think it likely would have been a shock whether she’d
been notified prior to the event, or when it happened, given that it seems Mrs J is of the view
that she shouldn’t have been charged at all. So even if I were to accept that NatWest didn’t
do enough to notify Mrs J that interest would be re-starting; I don’t think it likely this has had
much impact on Mrs J. I say this because ultimately, I’m of the view that it wasn’t
unreasonable of it to have restarted the interest; and therefore, there hasn’t been any impact
to the overall position of the account.

Mrs J has explained that she is still in financial difficulty, and she has been borrowing money
to pay the interest that is currently being applied to her account. In these situations, I would
expect NatWest to engage with Mrs J to find out more about her current situation in order for
it to be able to decide what support it might be able to offer her. I can see that, following the
final response letter sent to her in October 2025, NatWest sent Mrs J an income and
assessment form in the post for her to complete. As a starting point, this is what I would
have expected NatWest to have done. My remit to consider NatWest’s actions is only up
until it issued its final response letter in October 2025; so I can’t consider any alleged acts or
omissions of NatWest after this point. I say this as I don’t know if Mrs J has completed the
income and expenditure assessment or not, but I would expect Mrs J to do this before
NatWest can look to decide how it can help her. And I will also remind NatWest of its
obligation to treat Mrs J with forbearance moving forward.

I note that Mrs J has also provided this service with evidence to show that another lender
has written off her overdraft debt with it. But just because another lender has taken the
decision to do this, it doesn’t mean that NatWest has acted unfairly in not doing so. If Mrs J
believes she has reason for the debt to be written off, then she should contact NatWest
about this so it can consider her request.

Overall, while I’m sorry to disappoint Mrs J, I won’t be ordering NatWest to do anything more
for her in relation to the interest charged from June 2025 until it issued its final response to
her. I think it’s possible NatWest could have done more to appropriately communicate with
Mrs J in relation to the support from SST and re-starting interest; but even if I were to make
the finding that it could and should have done more here, it has already made a payment to
her of £100, which I think would be sufficient to recognise any distress and inconvenience
caused by its communication. And therefore, I won’t be asking NatWest to do anything more
for her.

My final decision
For the reasons set out above, I don’t uphold Mrs J’s complaint.
Under the rules of the Financial Ombudsman Service, I’m required to ask Mrs J to accept or
reject my decision before 30 June 2026.

Sophie Wilkinson

Ombudsman
